Tush, never tell me! I take it much unkindly / That thou, Iago, who hast had my purse / As if the strings were thine, shouldst know of this.
Oh, don't give me that! I'm really hurt that you, Iago, who've been spending my money as if it were your own, knew about this.
'Sblood, but you will not hear me. / If ever I did dream of such a matter, / Abhor me.
Damn it, you won't listen to me. If I ever imagined such a thing, you can hate me.
Thou told'st me thou didst hold him in thy hate.
You told me you hated him.

Despise me, if I do not. Three great ones of the city, / In personal suit to make me his lieutenant, / Off-capp'd to him; and, by the faith of man, / I know my price, I am worth no worse a place. / But he, as loving his own pride and purposes, / Evades them, with a bumbast circumstance / Horribly stuff'd with epithets of war, / And, in conclusion, / Nonsuits my mediators; for, "Certes," says he, / "I have already chose my officer." / And what was he? / Forsooth, a great arithmetician, / One Michael Cassio, a Florentine / (A fellow almost damn'd in a fair wife) / That never set a squadron in the field, / Nor the division of a battle knows / More than a spinster; unless the bookish theoric, / Wherein the toged consuls can propose / As masterly as he. Mere prattle without practice / Is all his soldiership. But he, sir, had the election; / And I, of whom his eyes had seen the proof / At Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on other grounds / Christian and heathen, must be belee'd and calm'd / By debitor and creditor. This counter-caster, / He, in good time, must his lieutenant be, / And I- God bless the mark!- his Moorship's ancient.

Despise me if I don't. Three important men of this city went to him personally, hats in hand, asking him to make me his lieutenant. And I swear, I know what I'm worth: I deserve no lower rank. But he, loving his own pride and his own plans, dodged them with a pompous, roundabout speech stuffed with military jargon, and in the end turned my supporters down. "Truly," he says, "I've already chosen my officer." And who was it? A real mathematician, Michael Cassio from Florence (a guy who's nearly ruined by a pretty woman), who has never led a squad in battle and knows no more about deploying troops than an old maid does. All he knows is book theory, which any toga-wearing politician can talk about as well as he can. His whole soldiering is talk without practice. But he got the job. And I, whom Othello saw prove myself at Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on other battlefields, Christian and pagan, have to be left dead in the water by a bookkeeper. This number-cruncher gets to be his lieutenant, and I (God help me!) am stuck as his Moorship's flag-bearer.
By heaven, I rather would have been his hangman.
By heaven, I'd rather have been his hangman.

Why, there's no remedy. 'Tis the curse of service, / Preferment goes by letter and affection, / And not by old gradation, where each second / Stood heir to the first. Now, sir, be judge yourself / Whether I in any just term am affined / To love the Moor.

Well, nothing can be done. That's the curse of military service: promotion comes through recommendation letters and favoritism, not the old system of seniority, where the second-in-line inherits the top spot. Now, sir, you judge for yourself whether I have any reason to love the Moor.
I would not follow him then.
Then I wouldn't serve under him.

O, sir, content you. / I follow him to serve my turn upon him: / We cannot all be masters, nor all masters / Cannot be truly follow'd. You shall mark / Many a duteous and knee-crooking knave, / That doting on his own obsequious bondage / Wears out his time, much like his master's ass, / For nought but provender, and when he's old, cashier'd. / Whip me such honest knaves. Others there are / Who, trimm'd in forms and visages of duty, / Keep yet their hearts attending on themselves, / And throwing but shows of service on their lords / Do well thrive by them; and when they have lined their coats / Do themselves homage. These fellows have some soul, / And such a one do I profess myself. / For, sir, / It is as sure as you are Roderigo, / Were I the Moor, I would not be Iago. / In following him, I follow but myself; / Heaven is my judge, not I for love and duty, / But seeming so, for my peculiar end. / For when my outward action doth demonstrate / The native act and figure of my heart / In complement extern, 'tis not long after / But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve / For daws to peck at: I am not what I am.

Oh, relax. I serve him so I can use him for my own ends. We can't all be masters, and not every master can be faithfully served. You've seen plenty of loyal, bowing servants who love their own slavish obedience and wear themselves out like their master's donkey, working for nothing but food, and when they're old they get fired. Whip those honest fools, I say. There are others who put on the costume and face of duty while keeping their hearts focused on themselves. They put on a show of service to their lords, profit from it, and once they've lined their pockets they serve only themselves. Those guys have some spirit, and I'm one of them. Because, sir, as sure as you're Roderigo, if I were the Moor, I wouldn't want to be Iago. In serving him, I'm really serving myself. Heaven knows I'm not doing it out of love and duty; I only seem to, for my own private purpose. Because when my outward actions start to reveal what's really in my heart, I might as well wear my heart on my sleeve for birds to peck at. I am not what I seem.
What a full fortune does the thick-lips owe, / If he can carry't thus!
What luck the thick-lipped Moor has, if he can pull this off!

Call up her father, / Rouse him, make after him, poison his delight, / Proclaim him in the streets, incense her kinsmen, / And, though he in a fertile climate dwell, / Plague him with flies. Though that his joy be joy, / Yet throw such changes of vexation on't / As it may lose some color.

Wake up her father. Rouse him, go after Othello, poison his happiness, denounce him in the streets, enrage her relatives. And even though he's living in paradise, plague him with flies. Even if his joy is real, hit it with so many troubles that it loses some of its shine.
Here is her father's house; I'll call aloud.
Here's her father's house. I'll shout.
Do, with like timorous accent and dire yell / As when, by night and negligence, the fire / Is spied in populous cities.
Do it, with the same terrified tone and awful yell as when a fire is spotted at night in a crowded city.
What, ho, Brabantio! Signior Brabantio, ho!
Awake! What, ho, Brabantio! Thieves! Thieves! Thieves! / Look to your house, your daughter, and your bags! / Thieves! Thieves!
Wake up! Hey, Brabantio! Thieves! Thieves! Thieves! Check your house, your daughter, and your money bags! Thieves! Thieves!
What is the reason of this terrible summons? / What is the matter there?
What's the reason for this terrible racket? What's going on out there?
Signior, is all your family within?
Sir, is your whole family inside?
Why? Why are you asking me this?

'Zounds, sir, you're robb'd! For shame, put on your gown; / Your heart is burst, you have lost half your soul; / Even now, now, very now, an old black ram / Is tupping your white ewe. Arise, arise! / Awake the snorting citizens with the bell, / Or else the devil will make a grandsire of you. / Arise, I say!

Damn it, sir, you've been robbed! For shame, put on your robe. Your heart is broken; you've lost half your soul. Right now, this very minute, an old black ram is mating with your white ewe. Get up, get up! Ring the bell and wake the snoring citizens, or the devil will make you a grandfather. Get up, I tell you!
What, have you lost your wits?
What, have you lost your mind?
Most reverend signior, do you know my voice?
Most respected sir, do you recognize my voice?

The worser welcome. / I have charged thee not to haunt about my doors. / In honest plainness thou hast heard me say / My daughter is not for thee; and now, in madness, / Being full of supper and distempering draughts, / Upon malicious bravery, dost thou come / To start my quiet.

All the less welcome. I've told you not to hang around my door. I've told you plainly that my daughter isn't for you. And now, out of your mind, full of dinner and too much drink, you come here out of spite to disturb my peace.
But thou must needs be sure / My spirit and my place have in them power / To make this bitter to thee.
But you can be sure that I have the temper and the position to make you regret this.
What tell'st thou me of robbing? This is Venice; / My house is not a grange.
What are you telling me about robbery? This is Venice. My house isn't some isolated farmhouse.
Most grave Brabantio, / In simple and pure soul I come to you.
Most honorable Brabantio, I come to you in good faith.

'Zounds, sir, you are one of those that will not serve God, / if the devil bid you. Because we come to do you service and you / think we are ruffians, you'll have your daughter covered with a / Barbary horse; you'll have your nephews neigh to you; you'll have / coursers for cousins, and gennets for germans.

Damn it, sir, you're the kind who won't serve God just because the devil tells you to. We come to do you a favor, and because you think we're thugs, you'll let your daughter be mounted by a North African horse. You'll have grandsons that neigh at you, and racehorses and ponies for relatives.
I am one, sir, that comes to tell you your daughter and the / Moor are now making the beast with two backs.
I'm someone, sir, who's come to tell you that your daughter and the Moor are right now making the beast with two backs.
This thou shalt answer; I know thee, Roderigo.
You'll pay for this. I know who you are, Roderigo.

Sir, I will answer anything. But, I beseech you, / If't be your pleasure and most wise consent, / As partly I find it is, that your fair daughter, / At this odd-even and dull watch o' the night, / Transported with no worse nor better guard / But with a knave of common hire, a gondolier, / To the gross clasps of a lascivious Moor- / If this be known to you, and your allowance, / We then have done you bold and saucy wrongs; / But if you know not this, my manners tell me / We have your wrong rebuke. Do not believe / That, from the sense of all civility, / I thus would play and trifle with your reverence. / Your daughter, if you have not given her leave, / I say again, hath made a gross revolt, / Tying her duty, beauty, wit, and fortunes / In an extravagant and wheeling stranger / Of here and everywhere. Straight satisfy yourself: / If she be in her chamber or your house, / Let loose on me the justice of the state / For thus deluding you.

Sir, I'll answer for anything. But please, if it's with your approval and wise consent (as it partly seems to be) that your lovely daughter, at this dead hour of the night, was carried off with no better protection than a hired gondolier into the crude embrace of a lustful Moor, if you know about this and allowed it, then we've done you a bold and rude wrong. But if you don't know, my manners tell me you're scolding us unfairly. Don't think I'd abandon all decency to play games with an honorable man like you. Your daughter, if you haven't given her permission, has committed a gross rebellion, tying her duty, beauty, intelligence, and fortune to a wandering foreigner with no home. Check for yourself right now: if she's in her room or in your house, let the law punish me for deceiving you.
Strike on the tinder, ho! / Give me a taper! Call up all my people! / This accident is not unlike my dream; / Belief of it oppresses me already. / Light, I say, light!
Strike a light! Give me a candle! Wake up all my servants! This is a lot like my dream. Just believing it is crushing me already. Light, I say, light!

Farewell, for I must leave you. / It seems not meet, nor wholesome to my place, / To be produced- as, if I stay, I shall- / Against the Moor; for I do know, the state, / However this may gall him with some check, / Cannot with safety cast him, for he's embark'd / With such loud reason to the Cyprus wars, / Which even now stands in act, that, for their souls, / Another of his fathom they have none / To lead their business; in which regard, / Though I do hate him as I do hell pains, / Yet for necessity of present life, / I must show out a flag and sign of love, / Which is indeed but sign. That you shall surely find him, / Lead to the Sagittary the raised search, / And there will I be with him. So farewell.

Goodbye; I have to leave you. It wouldn't be right, or good for my position, to be called as a witness against the Moor, which I will be if I stay. I know the state can't afford to dismiss him, even if this gets him a reprimand. He's been sent off with such urgency to the wars in Cyprus, which are already underway, that they couldn't find anyone else of his caliber to lead them if their souls depended on it. So even though I hate him like the pains of hell, for practical reasons I have to show a flag of loyalty, which really is just a flag. To be sure of finding him, lead the search party to the Sagittary inn. I'll be there with him. Goodbye.

It is too true an evil: gone she is, / And what's to come of my despised time / Is nought but bitterness. Now, Roderigo, / Where didst thou see her? O unhappy girl! / With the Moor, say'st thou? Who would be a father! / How didst thou know 'twas she? O, she deceives me / Past thought! What said she to you? Get more tapers. / Raise all my kindred. Are they married, think you?

It's horribly true. She's gone, and what's left of my miserable life will be nothing but bitterness. Now, Roderigo, where did you see her? Oh, unhappy girl! With the Moor, you say? Who would want to be a father! How did you know it was her? Oh, she's deceived me beyond belief! What did she say to you? Get more candles. Wake all my relatives. Do you think they're married?

O heaven! How got she out? O treason of the blood! / Fathers, from hence trust not your daughters' minds / By what you see them act. Is there not charms / By which the property of youth and maidhood / May be abused? Have you not read, Roderigo, / Of some such thing?

Oh heaven! How did she get out? Oh, betrayal by my own flesh and blood! Fathers, from now on, don't trust your daughters' minds just by how they act. Aren't there spells that can corrupt young virgins? Haven't you read about something like that, Roderigo?
Call up my brother. O, would you had had her! / Some one way, some another. Do you know / Where we may apprehend her and the Moor?
Wake up my brother. Oh, I wish you'd had her! Some of you go one way, some another. Do you know where we can catch her and the Moor?
I think I can discover him, if you please / To get good guard and go along with me.
I think I can find him, if you'll bring a good guard and come with me.
Pray you, lead on. At every house I'll call; / I may command at most. Get weapons, ho! / And raise some special officers of night. / On, good Roderigo, I'll deserve your pains.
Please, lead the way. I'll call at every house; most of them will obey me. Get weapons! And wake some of the night watch officers. Go on, good Roderigo. I'll reward you for your trouble.

Though in the trade of war I have slain men, / Yet do I hold it very stuff o' the conscience / To do no contrived murther. I lack iniquity / Sometimes to do me service. Nine or ten times / I had thought to have yerk'd him here under the ribs.

Though I've killed men in war, I still consider it a matter of conscience not to commit premeditated murder. Sometimes I'm not wicked enough for my own good. Nine or ten times I thought about stabbing him here, under the ribs.
It's better the way it is.

Nay, but he prated / And spoke such scurvy and provoking terms / Against your honor / That, with the little godliness I have, / I did full hard forbear him. But I pray you, sir, / Are you fast married? Be assured of this, / That the magnifico is much beloved, / And hath in his effect a voice potential / As double as the Duke's. He will divorce you, / Or put upon you what restraint and grievance / The law, with all his might to enforce it on, / Will give him cable.

No, but he went on and said such vile, provoking things about you that, with what little holiness I have, I could barely hold back. But tell me, sir, are you really married? Be sure of this: the old man is much loved here, and his influence is as powerful as the Duke's. He'll force a divorce, or put whatever restrictions and penalties on you the law allows, and he'll push it as far as it goes.

Let him do his spite. / My services, which I have done the signiory, / Shall out-tongue his complaints. 'Tis yet to know- / Which, when I know that boasting is an honor, / I shall promulgate- I fetch my life and being / From men of royal siege, and my demerits / May speak unbonneted to as proud a fortune / As this that I have reach'd. For know, Iago, / But that I love the gentle Desdemona, / I would not my unhoused free condition / Put into circumscription and confine / For the sea's worth. But, look! What lights come yond?

Let him do his worst. The services I've done for the state will drown out his complaints. People don't know yet (and I'll announce it only when boasting becomes honorable) that I come from royal ancestors, and my merits entitle me, without hat in hand, to as proud a fortune as the one I've won. Because know this, Iago: if I didn't love gentle Desdemona, I wouldn't give up my free, unattached life for all the treasure in the sea. But look! What are those lights over there?
Those are the raised father and his friends. / You were best go in.
That's her father, all worked up, and his friends. You'd better go inside.
Not I; I must be found. / My parts, my title, and my perfect soul / Shall manifest me rightly. Is it they?
Not me. I have to be found. My character, my rank, and my clear conscience will show me as I truly am. Is it them?
By Janus, I don't think so.
The servants of the Duke? And my lieutenant? / The goodness of the night upon you, friends! / What is the news?
The Duke's servants? And my lieutenant? Good evening, friends! What's the news?
The Duke does greet you, general, / And he requires your haste-post-haste appearance, / Even on the instant.
The Duke sends greetings, general, and he needs you to appear immediately, this very instant.
What is the matter, think you?
What's the matter, do you think?

Something from Cyprus, as I may divine; / It is a business of some heat. The galleys / Have sent a dozen sequent messengers / This very night at one another's heels; / And many of the consuls, raised and met, / Are at the Duke's already. You have been hotly call'd for, / When, being not at your lodging to be found, / The Senate hath sent about three several quests / To search you out.

Something from Cyprus, I'd guess. It's urgent business. The warships have sent a dozen messengers tonight, one right after the other, and many of the senators have been woken and are already at the Duke's. You've been urgently called for. When you weren't at your lodging, the Senate sent out three separate search parties to find you.
'Tis well I am found by you. / I will but spend a word here in the house / And go with you.
Good thing you found me. I'll just have a word inside here and then go with you.
Faith, he tonight hath boarded a land carack; / If it prove lawful prize, he's made forever.
Well, tonight he boarded a treasure ship on land. If it turns out to be a legal prize, he's made for life.
Marry, to- Come, captain, will you go?
Why, to— Come, captain, are you ready to go?
Here comes another troop to seek for you.
Here comes another group looking for you.
It is Brabantio. General, be advised, / He comes to bad intent.
It's Brabantio. General, be careful. He means trouble.
You, Roderigo! Come, sir, I am for you.
You, Roderigo! Come on, sir, I'll take you on.
Keep up your bright swords, for the dew will rust them. / Good signior, you shall more command with years / Than with your weapons.
Put away your shiny swords, or the dew will rust them. Good sir, your age will command more respect than your weapons.

O thou foul thief, where hast thou stow'd my daughter? / Damn'd as thou art, thou hast enchanted her, / For I'll refer me to all things of sense, / If she in chains of magic were not bound, / Whether a maid so tender, fair, and happy, / So opposite to marriage that she shunn'd / The wealthy, curled darlings of our nation, / Would ever have, to incur a general mock, / Run from her guardage to the sooty bosom / Of such a thing as thou- to fear, not to delight. / Judge me the world, if 'tis not gross in sense / That thou hast practiced on her with foul charms, / Abused her delicate youth with drugs or minerals / That weaken motion. I'll have't disputed on; / 'Tis probable, and palpable to thinking. / I therefore apprehend and do attach thee / For an abuser of the world, a practicer / Of arts inhibited and out of warrant. / Lay hold upon him. If he do resist, / Subdue him at his peril.

You filthy thief, where have you hidden my daughter? Damned as you are, you've bewitched her. I appeal to common sense: if she weren't bound by magic chains, would a girl so gentle, beautiful, and happy, so against marriage that she rejected the rich, curly-haired young men of our nation, ever run from her father's protection, making herself a public joke, to the sooty chest of a thing like you, something to fear, not to enjoy? Let the world judge if it isn't obvious that you've worked foul spells on her, abused her young innocence with drugs or potions that dull the senses. I'll have it tried in court. It's probable and obvious. So I arrest you as a corrupter of society, a practitioner of forbidden, illegal arts. Seize him. If he resists, subdue him by force.
Hold your hands, / Both you of my inclining and the rest. / Were it my cue to fight, I should have known it / Without a prompter. Where will you that I go / To answer this your charge?
Hold it, both my side and the rest of you. If it were my cue to fight, I'd have known it without a prompter. Where do you want me to go to answer your charge?
To prison, till fit time / Of law and course of direct session / Call thee to answer.
To prison, until the proper time when the law and a court session call you to answer.
What if I do obey? / How may the Duke be therewith satisfied, / Whose messengers are here about my side, / Upon some present business of the state / To bring me to him?
And if I obey? How would that satisfy the Duke, whose messengers are standing here beside me, to bring me to him on urgent state business?
'Tis true, most worthy signior; / The Duke's in council, and your noble self, / I am sure, is sent for.
It's true, most worthy sir. The Duke is in council, and I'm sure you've been sent for too.

How? The Duke in council? / In this time of the night? Bring him away; / Mine's not an idle cause. The Duke himself, / Or any of my brothers of the state, / Cannot but feel this wrong as 'twere their own; / For if such actions may have passage free, / Bond slaves and pagans shall our statesmen be.

What? The Duke in council at this time of night? Bring him along. My case isn't trivial. The Duke himself, or any of my fellow senators, can't help but feel this wrong as if it were their own. Because if things like this are allowed, slaves and heathens will end up running our government.
There is no composition in these news / That gives them credit.
There's no consistency in these reports to make them believable.
Indeed they are disproportion'd; / My letters say a hundred and seven galleys.
True, they don't match. My letters say a hundred and seven warships.
And mine, a hundred and forty.
And mine say a hundred and forty.

And mine, two hundred. / But though they jump not on a just account- / As in these cases, where the aim reports, / 'Tis oft with difference- yet do they all confirm / A Turkish fleet, and bearing up to Cyprus.
And mine, two hundred. But although they don't agree on the exact number (reports based on estimates often differ), they all confirm a Turkish fleet heading for Cyprus.
Nay, it is possible enough to judgement. / I do not so secure me in the error, / But the main article I do approve / In fearful sense.
Yes, that seems likely enough. I don't take false comfort from the discrepancies; I believe the main point, and it scares me.
[Within.] What, ho! What, ho! What, ho!
The Turkish preparation makes for Rhodes, / So was I bid report here to the state / By Signior Angelo.
The Turkish fleet is heading for Rhodes. Signior Angelo told me to report that to the government.
How say you by this change?
What do you make of this change?

This cannot be, / By no assay of reason; 'tis a pageant / To keep us in false gaze. When we consider / The importancy of Cyprus to the Turk, / And let ourselves again but understand / That as it more concerns the Turk than Rhodes, / So may he with more facile question bear it, / For that it stands not in such warlike brace, / But altogether lacks the abilities / That Rhodes is dress'd in. If we make thought of this, / We must not think the Turk is so unskillful / To leave that latest which concerns him first, / Neglecting an attempt of ease and gain, / To wake and wage a danger profitless.

It can't be, by any reasoning. It's a show to make us look the wrong way. When we consider how important Cyprus is to the Turks, and remember that it matters more to them than Rhodes does, and also that they can take it more easily because it isn't as well defended and lacks Rhodes's fortifications, if we think about this, we can't believe the Turk is so foolish as to leave until last what concerns him most, giving up an easy and profitable attack to stir up a pointless danger.
Nay, in all confidence, he's not for Rhodes.
Yes, I'm sure of it. He's not going for Rhodes.
The Ottomites, reverend and gracious, / Steering with due course toward the isle of Rhodes, / Have there injointed them with an after fleet.
Most honorable lords, the Turks, sailing straight for Rhodes, joined up there with a second fleet.
Ay, so I thought. How many, as you guess?
Yes, that's what I thought. How many ships, would you guess?

Of thirty sail; and now they do re-stem / Their backward course, bearing with frank appearance / Their purposes toward Cyprus. Signior Montano, / Your trusty and most valiant servitor, / With his free duty recommends you thus, / And prays you to believe him.

About thirty. And now they've turned around and are openly heading back toward Cyprus. Signior Montano, your loyal and brave servant, sends you this news with his respects and asks you to believe him.
'Tis certain then for Cyprus. / Marcus Luccicos, is not he in town?
Then it's definitely Cyprus. Is Marcus Luccicos in town?
Write from us to him, post-post-haste dispatch.
Write to him for us; send it with all possible speed.
Here comes Brabantio and the valiant Moor.
Here come Brabantio and the brave Moor.
Valiant Othello, we must straight employ you / Against the general enemy Ottoman. / [To Brabantio.] I did not see you; welcome, gentle signior; / We lack'd your counsel and your help tonight.
Brave Othello, we need to send you immediately against our common enemy, the Turks. [To Brabantio.] I didn't see you there; welcome, good sir. We missed your advice and help tonight.

So did I yours. Good your Grace, pardon me: / Neither my place nor aught I heard of business / Hath raised me from my bed, nor doth the general care / Take hold on me; for my particular grief / Is of so flood-gate and o'erbearing nature / That it engluts and swallows other sorrows, / And it is still itself.

And I missed yours. Your Grace, forgive me: it wasn't my position or any news of state business that got me out of bed, and public concerns don't grip me now. My personal grief is so overwhelming, like a flood through open gates, that it swallows up every other sorrow and remains just as huge.

Ay, to me. / She is abused, stol'n from me and corrupted / By spells and medicines bought of mountebanks; / For nature so preposterously to err, / Being not deficient, blind, or lame of sense, / Sans witchcraft could not.

Yes, to me. She's been abused, stolen from me, and corrupted by spells and potions bought from con men. For nature to go so absurdly wrong, when she isn't defective, blind, or stupid, would be impossible without witchcraft.

Whoe'er he be that in this foul proceeding / Hath thus beguiled your daughter of herself / And you of her, the bloody book of law / You shall yourself read in the bitter letter / After your own sense, yea, though our proper son / Stood in your action.

Whoever he is who has done this foul thing, robbing your daughter of her senses and you of her, you yourself shall read the harshest sentence from the bloody book of law, interpreted however you like, even if it were my own son you were accusing.
Humbly I thank your Grace. / Here is the man, this Moor, whom now, it seems, / Your special mandate for the state affairs / Hath hither brought.
I humbly thank your Grace. Here is the man: this Moor, who it seems you've summoned here for state affairs.
We're very sorry to hear it.
[To Othello.] What in your own part can you say to this?
[To Othello.] What can you say for yourself?

Most potent, grave, and reverend signiors, / My very noble and approved good masters, / That I have ta'en away this old man's daughter, / It is most true; true, I have married her; / The very head and front of my offending / Hath this extent, no more. Rude am I in my speech, / And little blest with the soft phrase of peace; / For since these arms of mine had seven years' pith, / Till now some nine moons wasted, they have used / Their dearest action in the tented field, / And little of this great world can I speak, / More than pertains to feats of broil and battle; / And therefore little shall I grace my cause / In speaking for myself. Yet, by your gracious patience, / I will a round unvarnish'd tale deliver / Of my whole course of love: what drugs, what charms, / What conjuration, and what mighty magic- / For such proceeding I am charged withal- / I won his daughter.

Most powerful, serious, and respected lords, my noble and proven masters: it's true that I've taken this old man's daughter. It's true; I've married her. That's the full extent of my offense, no more. I'm rough in my speech and not gifted with the smooth language of peacetime. Since I was seven years old, until about nine months ago, these arms have done their best work on the battlefield, and I can say little about the wider world beyond fighting and battle. So I won't help my case much by speaking for myself. Still, with your kind patience, I'll tell you a plain, unpolished story of my whole courtship: what drugs, what charms, what spells, and what powerful magic (since that's what I'm accused of) I used to win his daughter.

A maiden never bold, / Of spirit so still and quiet that her motion / Blush'd at herself; and she- in spite of nature, / Of years, of country, credit, everything- / To fall in love with what she fear'd to look on! / It is judgement maim'd and most imperfect, / That will confess perfection so could err / Against all rules of nature, and must be driven / To find out practices of cunning hell / Why this should be. I therefore vouch again / That with some mixtures powerful o'er the blood, / Or with some dram conjured to this effect, / He wrought upon her.

A girl who was never bold, so quiet and shy that she blushed at her own feelings. And she, against her nature, her age, her country, her reputation, everything, fell in love with what she was afraid to look at! Only a crippled and faulty judgment would claim that perfection could go so wrong against all the rules of nature. One has to look to the tricks of cunning hell to explain it. So I swear again that he worked on her with some potion that affects the blood, or some drug enchanted for this purpose.
To vouch this is no proof, / Without more certain and more overt test / Than these thin habits and poor likelihoods / Of modern seeming do prefer against him.
Swearing it isn't proof. You need clearer and more direct evidence than these flimsy appearances and weak assumptions you're bringing against him.
But, Othello, speak. / Did you by indirect and forced courses / Subdue and poison this young maid's affections? / Or came it by request, and such fair question / As soul to soul affordeth?
But Othello, speak. Did you use underhanded and forced methods to overpower and poison this young woman's affections? Or did it come through courtship and honest conversation, soul to soul?

I do beseech you, / Send for the lady to the Sagittary, / And let her speak of me before her father. / If you do find me foul in her report, / The trust, the office I do hold of you, / Not only take away, but let your sentence / Even fall upon my life.

I beg you, send for the lady at the Sagittary and let her speak about me in front of her father. If her account shows me guilty, don't just take away the trust and command you've given me: let your sentence fall on my life.
Ancient, conduct them; you best know the place.
Ensign, take them; you know the place best.
And till she come, as truly as to heaven / I do confess the vices of my blood, / So justly to your grave ears I'll present / How I did thrive in this fair lady's love / And she in mine.
And until she comes, as honestly as I confess my sins to heaven, I'll tell your serious ears how I won this fair lady's love, and she won mine.

Her father loved me, oft invited me, / Still question'd me the story of my life / From year to year, the battles, sieges, fortunes, / That I have pass'd. / I ran it through, even from my boyish days / To the very moment that he bade me tell it: / Wherein I spake of most disastrous chances, / Of moving accidents by flood and field, / Of hair-breadth 'scapes i' the imminent deadly breach, / Of being taken by the insolent foe / And sold to slavery, of my redemption thence / And portance in my travels' history; / Wherein of antres vast and deserts idle, / Rough quarries, rocks, and hills whose heads touch heaven, / It was my hint to speak- such was the process- / And of the Cannibals that each other eat, / The Anthropophagi, and men whose heads / Do grow beneath their shoulders. This to hear / Would Desdemona seriously incline; / But still the house affairs would draw her thence, / Which ever as she could with haste dispatch, / She'ld come again, and with a greedy ear / Devour up my discourse; which I observing, / Took once a pliant hour, and found good means / To draw from her a prayer of earnest heart / That I would all my pilgrimage dilate, / Whereof by parcels she had something heard, / But not intentively. I did consent, / And often did beguile her of her tears / When I did speak of some distressful stroke / That my youth suffer'd. My story being done, / She gave me for my pains a world of sighs; / She swore, in faith, 'twas strange, 'twas passing strange; / 'Twas pitiful, 'twas wondrous pitiful. / She wish'd she had not heard it, yet she wish'd / That heaven had made her such a man; she thank'd me, / And bade me, if I had a friend that loved her, / I should but teach him how to tell my story, / And that would woo her. Upon this hint I spake: / She loved me for the dangers I had pass'd, / And I loved her that she did pity them. / This only is the witchcraft I have used. / Here comes the lady; let her witness it.

Her father loved me and often invited me over. He kept asking me the story of my life, year by year: the battles, sieges, and fortunes I'd been through. I told it all, from my boyhood up to the moment he asked. I talked about terrible disasters, thrilling adventures at sea and on land, narrow escapes from death when the walls were breached, being captured by an arrogant enemy and sold into slavery, buying my freedom, and how I behaved in all my travels. I described huge caves and empty deserts, rough quarries, rocks, and mountains so high they touch heaven; that was my story. And I told of the cannibals who eat each other, the Anthropophagi, and men whose heads grow beneath their shoulders. Desdemona would lean in eagerly to hear all this. But household chores would keep pulling her away, and whenever she could finish them quickly, she'd come back and devour my words with a hungry ear. Noticing that, I found a good moment and got her to beg me sincerely to tell her my whole journey in full, since she'd only heard bits and pieces, not the whole story. I agreed, and often brought her to tears when I talked about some painful blow I suffered in my youth. When I finished, she gave me a world of sighs for my trouble. She swore it was strange, truly strange, pitiful, so incredibly pitiful. She wished she hadn't heard it, yet she wished heaven had made her a man like that. She thanked me and told me that if I had a friend who loved her, I should just teach him how to tell my story, and that would win her. With that hint, I spoke up. She loved me for the dangers I had been through, and I loved her because she pitied them. That's the only witchcraft I've used. Here comes the lady; let her confirm it.
I think this tale would win my daughter too. / Good Brabantio, / Take up this mangled matter at the best: / Men do their broken weapons rather use / Than their bare hands.
I think a story like that would win my daughter too. Good Brabantio, make the best of this messy situation. Men would rather fight with broken weapons than with their bare hands.

I pray you, hear her speak. / If she confess that she was half the wooer, / Destruction on my head, if my bad blame / Light on the man! Come hither, gentle mistress. / Do you perceive in all this noble company / Where most you owe obedience?
Please, hear her speak. If she admits she was half the wooer, let me be destroyed if I blame the man! Come here, gentle lady. Do you see, in this noble company, to whom you owe the most obedience?

My noble father, / I do perceive here a divided duty. / To you I am bound for life and education; / My life and education both do learn me / How to respect you; you are the lord of duty, / I am hitherto your daughter. But here's my husband, / And so much duty as my mother show'd / To you, preferring you before her father, / So much I challenge that I may profess / Due to the Moor, my lord.

My noble father, I see that my duty is divided here. To you I owe my life and upbringing, and both teach me to respect you. You're the one I owe duty to; so far I've been your daughter. But here is my husband. And just as much duty as my mother showed you, putting you before her own father, I claim the right to show to the Moor, my husband.

God be with you! I have done. / Please it your Grace, on to the state affairs; / I had rather to adopt a child than get it. / Come hither, Moor. / I here do give thee that with all my heart / Which, but thou hast already, with all my heart / I would keep from thee. For your sake, jewel, / I am glad at soul I have no other child; / For thy escape would teach me tyranny, / To hang clogs on them. I have done, my lord.

God be with you! I'm done. Your Grace, please, go on to the state business. I'd rather adopt a child than have one of my own. Come here, Moor. I give you, with all my heart, what I'd keep from you with all my heart if you didn't already have it. Because of you, my jewel, I'm glad in my soul I have no other children, because your escape would make me a tyrant, chaining them up. I'm done, my lord.

Let me speak like yourself, and lay a sentence / Which, as a grise or step, may help these lovers / Into your favor. / When remedies are past, the griefs are ended / By seeing the worst, which late on hopes depended. / To mourn a mischief that is past and gone / Is the next way to draw new mischief on. / What cannot be preserved when Fortune takes, / Patience her injury a mockery makes. / The robb'd that smiles steals something from the thief; / He robs himself that spends a bootless grief.

Let me speak as you would, and offer some wise sayings that might be a step to help these lovers back into your good graces. When there's no cure left, grief ends once we see the worst that we used to hope wouldn't happen. Mourning a misfortune that's past and gone is the surest way to bring a new one. When Fortune takes what can't be saved, patience makes a joke of the injury. The robbed man who smiles steals something back from the thief; the one who wastes time on useless grief robs himself.

So let the Turk of Cyprus us beguile; / We lose it not so long as we can smile. / He bears the sentence well, that nothing bears / But the free comfort which from thence he hears; / But he bears both the sentence and the sorrow / That, to pay grief, must of poor patience borrow. / These sentences, to sugar or to gall, / Being strong on both sides, are equivocal. / But words are words; I never yet did hear / That the bruised heart was pierced through the ear. / I humbly beseech you, proceed to the affairs of state.

So let the Turks cheat us out of Cyprus; we haven't lost it as long as we can smile. A man takes this advice well when it costs him nothing and he only hears the free comfort in it. But a man who must pay off his grief by borrowing from his poor patience has to bear both the advice and the sorrow. These sayings, sweet or bitter, cut both ways, so they mean nothing. Words are just words. I've never heard of a bruised heart being healed through the ear. I humbly beg you, go on with the affairs of state.

The Turk with a most mighty preparation makes for Cyprus. / Othello, the fortitude of the place is best known to you; and / though we have there a substitute of most allowed sufficiency, / yet opinion, a sovereign mistress of effects, throws a more safer / voice on you. You must therefore be content to slubber the gloss / of your new fortunes with this more stubborn and boisterous / expedition.

The Turk is heading for Cyprus with a huge force. Othello, you know that place's defenses best. Although we have a highly capable deputy there, public opinion, which ultimately decides things, has more confidence in you. So you'll have to accept tarnishing the shine of your new happiness with this rougher, more violent expedition.

The tyrant custom, most grave senators, / Hath made the flinty and steel couch of war / My thrice-driven bed of down. I do agnize / A natural and prompt alacrity / I find in hardness and do undertake / These present wars against the Ottomites. / Most humbly therefore bending to your state, / I crave fit disposition for my wife, / Due reference of place and exhibition, / With such accommodation and besort / As levels with her breeding.

Habit, that tyrant, most serious senators, has made the hard, stony, steel bed of war feel to me like the softest feather bed. I admit I feel a natural, eager readiness for hardship, and I take on this war against the Turks. So, humbly bowing to your authority, I ask for proper arrangements for my wife: suitable lodging, an allowance, and the kind of accommodation and company that fits her upbringing.
If you please, / Be't at her father's.
If you like, she can stay at her father's.

Nor I. I would not there reside / To put my father in impatient thoughts / By being in his eye. Most gracious Duke, / To my unfolding lend your prosperous ear, / And let me find a charter in your voice / To assist my simpleness.
Nor will I. I wouldn't live there and upset my father by being in his sight. Most gracious Duke, listen kindly to what I have to say, and let your support help my inexperience.

That I did love the Moor to live with him, / My downright violence and storm of fortunes / May trumpet to the world. My heart's subdued / Even to the very quality of my lord. / I saw Othello's visage in his mind, / And to his honors and his valiant parts / Did I my soul and fortunes consecrate. / So that, dear lords, if I be left behind, / A moth of peace, and he go to the war, / The rites for which I love him are bereft me, / And I a heavy interim shall support / By his dear absence. Let me go with him.

That I loved the Moor enough to live with him, my bold break with convention and my reckless gamble with my future can announce to the world. My heart has been won over by his very nature. I saw Othello's true face in his mind, and I dedicated my soul and fortune to his honor and his courage. So, dear lords, if I'm left behind, a useless moth living in peace while he goes to war, I'm robbed of the very things I love him for, and I'll have to endure a heavy wait in his absence. Let me go with him.

Let her have your voices. / Vouch with me, heaven, I therefore beg it not / To please the palate of my appetite, / Nor to comply with heat- the young affects / In me defunct- and proper satisfaction; / But to be free and bounteous to her mind. / And heaven defend your good souls, that you think / I will your serious and great business scant / For she is with me. No, when light-wing'd toys / Of feather'd Cupid seel with wanton dullness / My speculative and officed instruments, / That my disports corrupt and taint my business, / Let housewives make a skillet of my helm, / And all indign and base adversities / Make head against my estimation!

Give her your approval. Heaven be my witness, I don't ask this to satisfy my appetite or my passions (the urges of youth are dead in me) or for my own pleasure, but to be generous to her wishes. And heaven forbid you good men think I'll neglect your serious and important business because she's with me. No: if the light-winged toys of feathered Cupid ever blind my eyes and dull my mind with lust, so that my pleasures corrupt and spoil my work, let housewives turn my helmet into a cooking pot, and let every shameful and humiliating misfortune rise up against my reputation!
Be it as you shall privately determine, / Either for her stay or going. The affair cries haste, / And speed must answer't: you must hence tonight.
Decide it privately, whether she stays or goes. The situation is urgent and needs a fast response. You have to leave tonight.
At nine i' the morning here we'll meet again. / Othello, leave some officer behind, / And he shall our commission bring to you, / With such things else of quality and respect / As doth import you.
We'll meet here again at nine in the morning. Othello, leave an officer behind, and he'll bring you our official orders and whatever else concerns your rank and position.
So please your Grace, my ancient; / A man he is of honesty and trust. / To his conveyance I assign my wife, / With what else needful your good Grace shall think / To be sent after me.
If it please your Grace, my ensign. He's an honest and trustworthy man. I'll leave my wife in his care, along with anything else your Grace thinks should be sent after me.
Let it be so. / Good night to everyone. [To Brabantio.] And, noble signior, / If virtue no delighted beauty lack, / Your son-in-law is far more fair than black.
So be it. Good night, everyone. [To Brabantio.] And, noble sir, if goodness has its own beauty, your son-in-law is far more fair than black.
Adieu, brave Moor, use Desdemona well.
Goodbye, brave Moor. Treat Desdemona well.
Look to her, Moor, if thou hast eyes to see; / She has deceived her father, and may thee.
Keep an eye on her, Moor, if you have eyes to see. She deceived her father, and she may deceive you.

My life upon her faith! Honest Iago, / My Desdemona must I leave to thee. / I prithee, let thy wife attend on her, / And bring them after in the best advantage. / Come, Desdemona, I have but an hour / Of love, of worldly matters and direction, / To spend with thee. We must obey the time.

I'd bet my life on her loyalty! Honest Iago, I have to leave my Desdemona with you. Please have your wife look after her, and bring them after me when it's most convenient. Come, Desdemona, I have only an hour to spend with you on love, practical matters, and instructions. We must do what the time demands.
What do you say, noble heart?
What will I do, thinkest thou?
What do you think I'm going to do?
Why, go to bed and sleep.
Why, go to bed and sleep.
I'm going to drown myself immediately.
If thou dost, I shall never love thee after. / Why, thou silly gentleman!
If you do, I'll never like you again. Why, you silly gentleman!
It is silliness to live when to live is torment, and then / have we a prescription to die when death is our physician.
It's silly to live when living is torture. And we have a prescription to die when death is our doctor.

O villainous! I have looked upon the world for four times / seven years, and since I could distinguish betwixt a benefit and / an injury, I never found man that knew how to love himself. Ere I / would say I would drown myself for the love of a guinea hen, I / would change my humanity with a baboon.

Oh, nonsense! I've looked at the world for twenty-eight years, and ever since I could tell the difference between a benefit and an injury, I've never found a man who knew how to love himself. Before I'd say I'd drown myself for the love of some floozy, I'd trade my humanity with a baboon.
What should I do? I confess it is my shame to be so fond, / but it is not in my virtue to amend it.
What should I do? I admit it's shameful to be so infatuated, but I don't have the strength to fix it.

Virtue? a fig! 'Tis in ourselves that we are thus or thus. / Our bodies are gardens, to the which our wills are gardeners; so / that if we will plant nettles or sow lettuce, set hyssop and weed / up thyme, supply it with one gender of herbs or distract it with / many, either to have it sterile with idleness or manured with / industry, why, the power and corrigible authority of this lies in / our wills. If the balance of our lives had not one scale of / reason to poise another of sensuality, the blood and baseness of / our natures would conduct us to most preposterous conclusions. / But we have reason to cool our raging motions, our carnal stings, / our unbitted lusts; whereof I take this, that you call love, to / be a sect or scion.

Strength? Nonsense! It's up to us whether we're one way or another. Our bodies are gardens, and our wills are the gardeners. Whether we plant nettles or lettuce, grow hyssop or weed out thyme, fill it with one kind of herb or many, let it go barren through laziness or fertilize it with hard work, the power to control all this lies in our wills. If our lives didn't have reason on one side of the scale to balance our desires on the other, our lust and baser nature would lead us to absurd results. But we have reason to cool our raging urges, our sexual desires, our unbridled lusts. And I think what you call love is just an offshoot of that.

It is merely a lust of the blood and a permission of the / will. Come, be a man! Drown thyself? Drown cats and blind / puppies. I have professed me thy friend, and I confess me knit to / thy deserving with cables of perdurable toughness; I could never / better stead thee than now. Put money in thy purse; follow thou / the wars; defeat thy favor with an usurped beard. I say, put / money in thy purse. It cannot be that Desdemona should long / continue her love to the Moor- put money in thy purse- nor he his / to her. It was a violent commencement, and thou shalt see an / answerable sequestration- put but money in thy purse. These Moors / are changeable in their wills- fill thy purse with money. The / food that to him now is as luscious as locusts, shall be to him / shortly as acerb as the coloquintida. She must change for youth; / when she is sated with his body, she will find the error of her / choice. She must have change, she must; therefore put money in / thy purse. If thou wilt needs damn thyself, do it a more delicate / way than drowning. Make all the money thou canst. If sanctimony / and a frail vow betwixt an erring barbarian and a supersubtle / Venetian be not too hard for my wits and all the tribe of hell, / thou shalt enjoy her- therefore make money. A pox of drowning / thyself! It is clean out of the way. Seek thou rather to be / hanged in compassing thy joy than to be drowned and go without / her.

It's nothing but lust of the blood that the will allows. Come on, be a man! Drown yourself? Drown cats and blind puppies. I've said I'm your friend, and I admit I'm bound to you with unbreakable cables. I've never been more useful to you than now. Put money in your wallet. Follow the army to the wars. Disguise your face with a fake beard. I'm telling you, put money in your wallet. Desdemona can't go on loving the Moor for long (put money in your wallet), nor he her. It started violently, and you'll see it end just as abruptly (just put money in your wallet). These Moors are fickle (fill your wallet with money). The food that tastes as sweet as candy to him now will soon taste as bitter as poison. She'll want someone younger. When she's had enough of his body, she'll realize her mistake. She has to have a change, she must, so put money in your wallet. If you're set on damning yourself, do it in a more pleasant way than drowning. Raise all the money you can. If a holy ceremony and a fragile vow between a wandering barbarian and an overly clever Venetian girl aren't too much for my wits and all the powers of hell, you'll have her. So make money. To hell with drowning yourself! It's completely beside the point. You'd be better off being hanged for getting what you want than drowning without her.
Wilt thou be fast to my hopes, if I depend on the issue?
Will you stand by me if I count on this working out?

Thou art sure of me- go, make money. I have told thee often, / and I retell thee again and again, I hate the Moor. My cause is / hearted; thine hath no less reason. Let us be conjunctive in our / revenge against him. If thou canst cuckold him, thou dost thyself / a pleasure, me a sport. There are many events in the womb of time / which will be delivered. Traverse, go, provide thy money. We will / have more of this tomorrow. Adieu.

You can count on me. Go, raise money. I've told you often, and I'll tell you again and again: I hate the Moor. My reasons come from the heart; yours are just as strong. Let's join together in revenge against him. If you can sleep with his wife, you get pleasure and I get a laugh. Time is pregnant with many events that will be born. Go on, march! Get your money. We'll talk more tomorrow. Goodbye.
Where shall we meet i' the morning?
Where should we meet in the morning?
Go to, farewell. Do you hear, Roderigo?
Go on, goodbye. Do you hear me, Roderigo?
No more of drowning, do you hear?
No more talk of drowning, you hear?
I am changed; I'll go sell all my land.
I've changed my mind. I'll go sell all my land.

Thus do I ever make my fool my purse; / For I mine own gain'd knowledge should profane / If I would time expend with such a snipe / But for my sport and profit. I hate the Moor, / And it is thought abroad that 'twixt my sheets / He has done my office. I know not if't be true, / But I for mere suspicion in that kind / Will do as if for surety. He holds me well, / The better shall my purpose work on him. / Cassio's a proper man. Let me see now- / To get his place, and to plume up my will / In double knavery- How, how?- Let's see- / After some time, to abuse Othello's ear / That he is too familiar with his wife. / He hath a person and a smooth dispose / To be suspected- framed to make women false. / The Moor is of a free and open nature, / That thinks men honest that but seem to be so, / And will as tenderly be led by the nose / As asses are. / I have't. It is engender'd. Hell and night / Must bring this monstrous birth to the world's light.

This is how I always make my fool pay my way. I'd be wasting what I've learned if I spent time with such an idiot except for my own fun and profit. I hate the Moor. And people say he's slept with my wife. I don't know if it's true, but just the suspicion is enough for me; I'll act as if it were certain. He thinks well of me; that will make my plan work on him all the better. Cassio's a handsome man. Let me see now: how to get his job and pull off my plan in a double scam. How? How? Let's see. After a while, I'll whisper in Othello's ear that Cassio is too familiar with his wife. Cassio has the looks and smooth manner to be suspected; he's made to make women unfaithful. The Moor is open and trusting by nature. He thinks men are honest if they only seem to be, and he can be led by the nose as easily as a donkey. I've got it. It's conceived. Hell and darkness must bring this monstrous birth into the light of the world.
What from the cape can you discern at sea?
What can you see out at sea from the cliff?
Nothing at all. It is a high-wrought flood; / I cannot, 'twixt the heaven and the main, / Descry a sail.
Nothing at all. The waves are huge. I can't spot a single sail between the sky and the sea.

Methinks the wind hath spoke aloud at land; / A fuller blast ne'er shook our battlements. / If it hath ruffian'd so upon the sea, / What ribs of oak, when mountains melt on them, / Can hold the mortise? What shall we hear of this?

I think the wind has roared loudly on land too; a stronger gust never shook our walls. If it has been this violent at sea, what oak ships can hold together when mountains of water crash down on them? What news will we hear after this?

A segregation of the Turkish fleet. / For do but stand upon the foaming shore, / The chidden billow seems to pelt the clouds; / The wind-shaked surge, with high and monstrous mane, / Seems to cast water on the burning bear, / And quench the guards of the ever-fixed pole. / I never did like molestation view / On the enchafed flood.

That the Turkish fleet has been scattered. Just stand on the foaming shore: the battered waves seem to hit the clouds, and the wind-whipped surge, with its huge monstrous mane, seems to throw water on the stars of the Great Bear and put out the stars that guard the fixed North Star. I've never seen such turmoil on the raging sea.
If that the Turkish fleet / Be not enshelter'd and embay'd, they are drown'd; / It is impossible to bear it out.
If the Turkish fleet isn't sheltered in some bay, they've drowned. They can't possibly ride this out.

News, lads! Our wars are done. / The desperate tempest hath so bang'd the Turks, / That their designment halts. A noble ship of Venice / Hath seen a grievous wreck and sufferance / On most part of their fleet.
News, men! Our war is over. This furious storm has smashed the Turks so badly that their plans are finished. A noble ship from Venice saw most of their fleet wrecked and ruined.
The ship is here put in, / A Veronesa. Michael Cassio, / Lieutenant to the warlike Moor, Othello, / Is come on shore; the Moor himself at sea, / And is in full commission here for Cyprus.

The ship has docked here, a ship from Verona. Michael Cassio, lieutenant to the warlike Moor Othello, has come ashore. The Moor himself is still at sea, and he's been given full command here in Cyprus.
I am glad on't; 'tis a worthy governor.
I'm glad. He's a worthy governor.
But this same Cassio, though he speak of comfort / Touching the Turkish loss, yet he looks sadly / And prays the Moor be safe; for they were parted / With foul and violent tempest.
But this Cassio, though he brings good news about the Turkish losses, looks worried and prays the Moor is safe, because they were separated by a terrible, violent storm.

Pray heavens he be, / For I have served him, and the man commands / Like a full soldier. Let's to the seaside, ho! / As well to see the vessel that's come in / As to throw out our eyes for brave Othello, / Even till we make the main and the aerial blue / An indistinct regard.

I pray to heaven he is. I've served under him, and the man commands like a true soldier. Let's go to the shore! We'll see the ship that's come in, and look out for brave Othello until the sea and the sky blur together.
Come, let's do so, / For every minute is expectancy / Of more arrivance.
Come on, let's go. Any minute now more ships could arrive.
Thanks, you the valiant of this warlike isle, / That so approve the Moor! O, let the heavens / Give him defense against the elements, / For I have lost him on a dangerous sea.
Thank you, brave men of this warlike island, for praising the Moor so highly! Oh, may the heavens protect him from the elements, because I lost him on a dangerous sea.
His bark is stoutly timber'd, and his pilot / Of very expert and approved allowance; / Therefore my hopes, not surfeited to death, / Stand in bold cure.
His ship is solidly built, and his pilot is highly skilled and experienced. So my hopes, which aren't yet dead, are still strong.
The town is empty; on the brow o' the sea / Stand ranks of people, and they cry, "A sail!"
The town is empty. Crowds of people stand on the cliff by the sea, and they're shouting, "A sail!"
My hopes do shape him for the governor.
They do discharge their shot of courtesy- / Our friends at least.
They're firing a friendly salute. At least they're friends.
I pray you, sir, go forth, / And give us truth who 'tis that is arrived.
Please, sir, go and tell us truthfully who has arrived.
But, good lieutenant, is your general wived?
But, good lieutenant, is your general married?

Most fortunately: he hath achieved a maid / That paragons description and wild fame, / One that excels the quirks of blazoning pens, / And in the essential vesture of creation / Does tire the ingener.

Very luckily. He has won a woman who surpasses any description or wild rumor, who outdoes the flourishes of the most flattering writers, and whose natural beauty would exhaust any artist trying to praise it.
How now! who has put in?
'Tis one Iago, ancient to the general.

He has had most favorable and happy speed: / Tempests themselves, high seas, and howling winds, / The gutter'd rocks, and congregated sands, / Traitors ensteep'd to clog the guiltless keel, / As having sense of beauty, do omit / Their mortal natures, letting go safely by / The divine Desdemona.

He's had a very quick and lucky voyage. Storms, high seas, howling winds, jagged rocks, and sandbars (traitors lying underwater to trap innocent ships) all seem to have a sense of beauty and set aside their deadly nature to let the divine Desdemona pass safely.

She that I spake of, our great captain's captain, / Left in the conduct of the bold Iago, / Whose footing here anticipates our thoughts / A se'nnight's speed. Great Jove, Othello guard, / And swell his sail with thine own powerful breath, / That he may bless this bay with his tall ship, / Make love's quick pants in Desdemona's arms, / Give renew'd fire to our extincted spirits, / And bring all Cyprus comfort.

The one I told you about, our great captain's captain, left in the care of bold Iago. He's arrived a week sooner than we expected. Great Jove, protect Othello and fill his sail with your own powerful breath, so he can bless this bay with his tall ship, breathe quick with love in Desdemona's arms, give new fire to our dampened spirits, and bring comfort to all of Cyprus.

O, behold, / The riches of the ship is come on shore! / Ye men of Cyprus, let her have your knees. / Hall to thee, lady! And the grace of heaven, / Before, behind thee, and on every hand, / Enwheel thee round!
Oh, look! The ship's treasure has come ashore! Men of Cyprus, kneel to her. Hail to you, lady! May heaven's grace surround you, in front, behind, and on every side!
I thank you, valiant Cassio. / What tidings can you tell me of my lord?
Thank you, brave Cassio. What news can you give me of my husband?
He is not yet arrived, nor know I aught / But that he's well and will be shortly here.
He hasn't arrived yet. All I know is that he's well and will be here soon.
O, but I fear- How lost you company?
Oh, but I'm afraid... How did you get separated?
The great contention of the sea and skies / Parted our fellowship- But, hark! a sail.
The great battle between the sea and the sky split us up. But listen! A ship.
They give their greeting to the citadel; / This likewise is a friend.
They're saluting the fort. This one's a friend too.

Good ancient, you are welcome. [To Emilia.] Welcome, mistress. / Let it not gall your patience, good Iago, / That I extend my manners; 'tis my breeding / That gives me this bold show of courtesy. [Kisses her.]
Good ensign, welcome. [To Emilia.] Welcome, madam. Don't be offended, good Iago, that I'm being so forward with my manners. It's my upbringing that makes me show such bold courtesy. [Kisses her.]
Sir, would she give you so much of her lips / As of her tongue she oft bestows on me, / You'ld have enough.
Sir, if she gave you as much of her lips as she gives me of her tongue, you'd have had enough.
Come on, she hardly says anything.
In faith, too much; / I find it still when I have list to sleep. / Marry, before your ladyship I grant, / She puts her tongue a little in her heart / And chides with thinking.
Honestly, she says too much. I notice it whenever I want to sleep. Of course, in front of you, my lady, I admit she bites her tongue a bit and only scolds in her thoughts.
You have little cause to say so.
You have no reason to say that.

Come on, come on. You are pictures out of doors, / Bells in your parlors, wildcats in your kitchens, / Saints in your injuries, devils being offended, / Players in your housewifery, and housewives in your beds.

Come on, come on. You women are pretty as pictures in public, chattering like bells in your living rooms, wildcats in your kitchens. You act like saints when you hurt someone, and like devils when someone offends you. You play at keeping house, and you're only serious about business in bed.
Oh, shame on you, you slanderer!
Nay, it is true, or else I am a Turk: / You rise to play, and go to bed to work.
No, it's true, or I'm a Turk. You get up to play and go to bed to work.
You shall not write my praise.
I won't have you write my praises.
What wouldst thou write of me, if thou shouldst / praise me?
What would you write about me, if you had to praise me?
O gentle lady, do not put me to't, / For I am nothing if not critical.
Oh, gentle lady, don't ask me to. I'm nothing if not critical.
Come on, assay- There's one gone to the harbor?
Come on, try. Has someone gone to the harbor?
I am not merry, but I do beguile / The thing I am by seeming otherwise. / Come, how wouldst thou praise me?
I'm not cheerful, but I'm distracting myself from how I feel by pretending otherwise. Come on, how would you praise me?

I am about it, but indeed my invention / Comes from my pate as birdlime does from frieze; / It plucks out brains and all. But my Muse labors, / And thus she is deliver'd. / If she be fair and wise, fairness and wit, / The one's for use, the other useth it.

I'm working on it, but my ideas come out of my head like glue off a wool cloth: they pull my brains out with them. But my Muse is in labor, and here's what she gives birth to: If a woman is fair and wise, with beauty and brains, her beauty is for using, and her brains know how to use it.
Well praised! How if she be black and witty?
Nicely praised! What if she's dark and clever?
If she be black, and thereto have a wit, / She'll find a white that shall her blackness fit.
If she's dark and also clever, she'll find a fair man who fits her darkness.
What if she's beautiful and foolish?
She never yet was foolish that was fair, / For even her folly help'd her to an heir.
No beautiful woman was ever foolish, because her foolishness helped her get a child.
These are old fond paradoxes to make fools laugh i' the / alehouse. What miserable praise hast thou for her that's foul and / foolish?
These are silly old jokes to make fools laugh in the pub. What awful praise do you have for a woman who's ugly and foolish?
There's none so foul and foolish thereunto, / But does foul pranks which fair and wise ones do.
No woman is so ugly and foolish that she doesn't get up to the same dirty tricks the beautiful and wise ones do.

O heavy ignorance! Thou praisest the worst best. But what / praise couldst thou bestow on a deserving woman indeed, one that / in the authority of her merit did justly put on the vouch of very / malice itself?
Oh, what ignorance! You praise the worst one best. But what praise could you give a truly deserving woman, one so good that even malice itself would have to admit her worth?

She that was ever fair and never proud, / Had tongue at will and yet was never loud, / Never lack'd gold and yet went never gay, / Fled from her wish and yet said, "Now I may"; / She that, being anger'd, her revenge being nigh, / Bade her wrong stay and her displeasure fly; / She that in wisdom never was so frail / To change the cod's head for the salmon's tail; / She that could think and ne'er disclose her mind, / See suitors following and not look behind; / She was a wight, if ever such wight were-

A woman who was always beautiful but never proud, who could speak her mind but was never loud, who always had money but never dressed flashy, who held back from what she wanted even when she could have it; a woman who, when angered and able to take revenge, let the insult go and her anger fade; a woman who was never so foolish as to trade something good for something worthless; who could think without blurting out her thoughts, and could have men chasing her without looking back. She'd be the kind of woman, if such a woman ever existed...
To suckle fools and chronicle small beer.
To breastfeed idiots and keep track of trivial household accounts.
O most lame and impotent conclusion! Do not learn of him, / Emilia, though he be thy husband. How say you, Cassio? Is he not / a most profane and liberal counselor?
Oh, what a lame and feeble ending! Don't learn from him, Emilia, even if he is your husband. What do you think, Cassio? Isn't he a crude, foul-mouthed advisor?
He speaks home, madam. You may relish him more in the / soldier than in the scholar.
He speaks bluntly, madam. You'll appreciate him more as a soldier than as a scholar.

[Aside.] He takes her by the palm; ay, well said, whisper. / With as little a web as this will I ensnare as great a fly as / Cassio. Ay, smile upon her, do; I will gyve thee in thine own / courtship. You say true; 'tis so, indeed. If such tricks as these / strip you out of your lieutenantry, it had been better you had / not kissed your three fingers so oft, which now again you are / most apt to play the sir in. Very good. Well kissed! an excellent / courtesy! 'tis so, indeed. Yet again your fingers to your lips? / Would they were clyster-pipes for your sake! [Trumpet within.] / The Moor! I know his trumpet.

[Aside.] He takes her by the hand. Yes, that's it, whisper. With a web this small I'll catch a fly as big as Cassio. Yes, smile at her, go on. I'll trap you in your own courtly manners. That's right, exactly. If tricks like these cost you your lieutenancy, you'd have been better off not kissing your fingers so often, which you're now so eager to do again like a fine gentleman. Very good. Nicely kissed! Excellent manners! Exactly. Your fingers to your lips again? I wish they were enema tubes, for your sake! [Trumpet offstage.] The Moor! I know his trumpet.
Let's meet him and receive him.

It gives me wonder great as my content / To see you here before me. O my soul's joy! / If after every tempest come such calms, / May the winds blow till they have waken'd death! / And let the laboring bark climb hills of seas / Olympus-high, and duck again as low / As hell's from heaven! If it were now to die, / 'Twere now to be most happy; for I fear / My soul hath her content so absolute / That not another comfort like to this / Succeeds in unknown fate.

It's as amazing as it is wonderful to find you here before me. Oh, my soul's joy! If every storm is followed by a calm like this, let the winds blow until they wake the dead! Let the struggling ship climb mountains of waves as high as Olympus and then drop as low as hell is from heaven! If I were to die right now, I'd die the happiest man alive, because I'm afraid my soul is so completely content that I'll never feel happiness like this again in my unknown future.
The heavens forbid / But that our loves and comforts should increase, / Even as our days do grow!
Heaven forbid! May our love and happiness only grow as our days go on!

Amen to that, sweet powers! / I cannot speak enough of this content; / It stops me here; it is too much of joy. / And this, and this, the greatest discords be [Kisses her.] / That e'er our hearts shall make!
Amen to that, sweet heaven! I can't say enough about how happy I am. It catches me here; it's too much joy. And may this, and this [Kisses her], be the worst conflict our hearts ever have!
[Aside.] O, you are well tuned now! / But I'll set down the pegs that make this music, / As honest as I am.
[Aside.] Oh, you're in perfect harmony now! But I'll loosen the strings that make this music, as honest as I am.

Come, let us to the castle. / News, friends: our wars are done, the Turks are drown'd. / How does my old acquaintance of this isle? / Honey, you shall be well desired in Cyprus; / I have found great love amongst them. O my sweet, / I prattle out of fashion, and I dote / In mine own comforts. I prithee, good Iago, / Go to the bay and disembark my coffers. / Bring thou the master to the citadel; / He is a good one, and his worthiness / Does challenge much respect. Come, Desdemona, / Once more well met at Cyprus.

Come, let's go to the castle. News, friends: the war is over; the Turks have drowned. How are my old friends on this island? Darling, you'll be very welcome in Cyprus; I've found great affection here. Oh, my sweet, I'm babbling and going on about my own happiness. Please, good Iago, go to the bay and unload my chests. Bring the ship's captain to the fort; he's a good man, and his ability deserves a lot of respect. Come, Desdemona. Once again, welcome to Cyprus.

Do thou meet me presently at the harbor. Come hither. If thou / be'st valiant- as they say base men being in love have then a / nobility in their natures more than is native to them- list me. / The lieutenant tonight watches on the court of guard. First, I / must tell thee this: Desdemona is directly in love with him.

Meet me at the harbor right away. Come here. If you're brave (and they say even lowborn men get a nobility from being in love that they don't normally have), listen to me. The lieutenant is on guard duty tonight. First, I have to tell you this: Desdemona is definitely in love with him.

Lay thy finger thus, and let thy soul be instructed. Mark me / with what violence she first loved the Moor, but for bragging and / telling her fantastical lies. And will she love him still for / prating? Let not thy discreet heart think it. Her eye must be / fed; and what delight shall she have to look on the devil? When / the blood is made dull with the act of sport, there should be, / again to inflame it and to give satiety a fresh appetite, / loveliness in favor, sympathy in years, manners, and beauties- / all which the Moor is defective in. Now, for want of these / required conveniences, her delicate tenderness will find itself / abused, begin to heave the gorge, disrelish and abhor the Moor; / very nature will instruct her in it and compel her to some second / choice. Now sir, this granted- as it is a most pregnant and / unforced position- who stands so eminently in the degree of this / fortune as Cassio does? A knave very voluble; no further / conscionable than in putting on the mere form of civil and humane / seeming, for the better compass of his salt and most hidden loose / affection? Why, none, why, none- a slipper and subtle knave, a / finder out of occasions, that has an eye can stamp and / counterfeit advantages, though true advantage never present / itself- a devilish knave! Besides, the knave is handsome, young, / and hath all those requisites in him that folly and green minds / look after- a pestilent complete knave, and the woman hath found / him already.

Put your finger to your lips like this, and let your soul learn something. Remember how violently she first loved the Moor, just because he bragged and told her fantastic lies. Will she keep loving him for his chatter? Don't you believe it. Her eyes need feeding, and what pleasure will she get from looking at the devil? When sex has dulled the passion, it takes good looks, a similar age, manners, and beauty to rekindle it and give a full stomach a fresh appetite, and the Moor lacks all of these. Without these necessary qualities, her delicate sensibilities will feel cheated. She'll start to feel sick, lose her taste for the Moor, and loathe him. Nature itself will teach her this and push her to a second choice. Now, sir, given that (and it's a very obvious and natural conclusion), who is better placed to get lucky than Cassio? A smooth-talking rascal, with no more conscience than it takes to put on a show of politeness and manners to hide his lustful, secret desires. Nobody, nobody! A slippery, cunning rascal, an opportunist, with an eye that can create and fake opportunities even when no real ones exist. A devilish rascal! Besides, he's handsome, young, and has everything that foolish, inexperienced women look for. A thoroughly rotten rascal, and the woman has already got her eye on him.
I cannot believe that in her; she's full of most blest / condition.
I can't believe that of her. She's full of the most blessed qualities.

Blest fig's-end! The wine she drinks is made of grapes. If / she had been blest, she would never have loved the Moor. Blest / pudding! Didst thou not see her paddle with the palm of his hand? / Didst not mark that?

Blessed nonsense! The wine she drinks is made of grapes like anyone else's. If she were so blessed, she'd never have loved the Moor. Blessed pudding! Didn't you see her stroking the palm of his hand? Didn't you notice that?
Yes, that I did; but that was but courtesy.
Yes, I did, but that was just politeness.

Lechery, by this hand; an index and obscure prologue to the / history of lust and foul thoughts. They met so near with their / lips that their breaths embraced together. Villainous thoughts, / Roderigo! When these mutualities so marshal the way, hard at hand / comes the master and main exercise, the incorporate conclusion. / Pish! But, sir, be you ruled by me. I have brought you from / Venice. Watch you tonight; for the command, I'll lay't upon you. / Cassio knows you not. I'll not be far from you. Do you find some / occasion to anger Cassio, either by speaking too loud, or / tainting his discipline, or from what other course you please, / which the time shall more favorably minister.

It was lust, I swear by this hand. A preview and secret prologue to a story of lust and dirty thoughts. Their lips came so close that their breath embraced. Villainous thoughts, Roderigo! When these intimacies lead the way, soon after comes the main event, the joining of bodies. Disgusting! But, sir, do as I say. I brought you from Venice. Be on guard duty tonight; I'll arrange for you to be posted. Cassio doesn't know you. I won't be far away. Find some way to make Cassio angry, either by talking too loudly, or mocking his discipline, or any other way you like that the moment offers.

Sir, he is rash and very sudden in choler, and haply may / strike at you.
