My friend is dead, 'tis done at your request; / But let her live.
My friend is dead; it's done, since you ask. But let her live.
Damn her, lewd minx! O, damn her! / Come, go with me apart; I will withdraw, / To furnish me with some swift means of death / For the fair devil. Now art thou my lieutenant.
Damn her, the lewd slut! Oh, damn her! Come, come away with me. I'll go and figure out some quick way to kill the beautiful devil. Now you're my lieutenant.
Do you know, sirrah, where Lieutenant Cassio lies?
Do you know, fellow, where Lieutenant Cassio lies?
I dare not say he lies anywhere.
I wouldn't dare say he lies anywhere.
He's a soldier; and for one to say a soldier lies, is / stabbing.
He's a soldier, and if you say a soldier lies, he'll stab you.
Come on! Where is he staying?
To tell you where he lodges, is to tell you where I lie.
To tell you where he's staying would be telling you where I lie.
Can anything be made of this?
Can anyone make sense of this?
I know not where he lodges, and for me to devise a lodging, / and say he lies here or he lies there, were to lie in mine own / throat.
I don't know where he's staying, and if I made up a place and said he lies here or lies there, I'd be lying through my teeth.
Can you inquire him out and be edified by report?
Can you ask around for him and find out?
I will catechize the world for him; that is, make questions / and by them answer.
I'll quiz the whole world for him, which means I'll ask questions and then answer them myself.
Seek him, bid him come hither. Tell him I have moved my / lord on his behalf and hope all will be well.
Find him and tell him to come here. Tell him I've spoken to my husband on his behalf and I hope everything will be fine.
To do this is within the compass of man's wit, and therefore / I will attempt the doing it.
Doing this is within a man's abilities, so I'll attempt it.
Where should I lose that handkerchief, Emilia?
Where could I have lost that handkerchief, Emilia?

Believe me, I had rather have lost my purse / Full of crusadoes; and, but my noble Moor / Is true of mind and made of no such baseness / As jealous creatures are, it were enough / To put him to ill thinking.

Believe me, I'd rather have lost my purse full of gold coins. If my noble Moor weren't so honest-minded and free of the meanness that jealous people have, it would be enough to make him think bad thoughts.
Who, he? I think the sun where he was born / Drew all such humors from him.
Who, him? I think the sun where he was born dried all those moods out of him.
I will not leave him now till Cassio / Be call'd to him.
I won't leave him alone now until Cassio is called back to him.
How is't with you, my lord?
Well, my good lady. [Aside.] O, hardness to dissemble! / How do you, Desdemona?
Fine, my good lady. [Aside.] Oh, how hard it is to pretend! How are you, Desdemona?
Give me your hand. This hand is moist, my lady.
Give me your hand. This hand is moist, my lady.
It yet has felt no age nor known no sorrow.
It hasn't felt age or known sorrow yet.

This argues fruitfulness and liberal heart; / Hot, hot, and moist. This hand of yours requires / A sequester from liberty, fasting, and prayer, / Much castigation, exercise devout, / For here's a young and sweating devil here / That commonly rebels. 'Tis a good hand, / A frank one.

This suggests a passionate and generous heart. Hot, hot, and moist. This hand of yours needs to be kept away from freedom, with fasting and prayer, a lot of discipline, and religious exercise, because there's a young, sweating devil here that often rebels. It's a good hand, a very open one.
You may, indeed, say so; / For 'twas that hand that gave away my heart.
You can certainly say that, because it was that hand that gave my heart away.
A liberal hand. The hearts of old gave hands; / But our new heraldry is hands, not hearts.
A generous hand. In the old days, people gave their hands along with their hearts. But in today's fashion, it's hands without hearts.
I cannot speak of this. Come now, your promise.
I don't know about that. Come now, your promise.
I have sent to bid Cassio come speak with you.
I've sent for Cassio to come and speak with you.
I have a salt and sorry rheum offends me; / Lend me thy handkerchief.
I have an annoying runny nose that's bothering me. Lend me your handkerchief.
I have it not about me.
I don't have it with me.

That's a fault. That handkerchief / Did an Egyptian to my mother give; / She was a charmer, and could almost read / The thoughts of people. She told her, while she kept it, / 'Twould make her amiable and subdue my father / Entirely to her love, but if she lost it / Or made a gift of it, my father's eye / Should hold her loathed and his spirits should hunt / After new fancies. She dying gave it me, / And bid me, when my fate would have me wive, / To give it her. I did so, and take heed on't; / Make it a darling like your precious eye; / To lose't or give't away were such perdition / As nothing else could match.

That's a mistake. An Egyptian woman gave that handkerchief to my mother. She was a sorceress who could almost read people's minds. She told my mother that as long as she kept it, it would make her desirable and keep my father completely in love with her. But if she lost it or gave it away, my father would look at her with disgust and his desires would go chasing after new loves. When she was dying, she gave it to me and told me to give it to my wife when I married. I did, so take good care of it. Treasure it like your own precious eyes. To lose it or give it away would be a disaster like no other.

'Tis true; there's magic in the web of it. / A sibyl, that had number'd in the world / The sun to course two hundred compasses, / In her prophetic fury sew'd the work; / The worms were hallow'd that did breed the silk, / And it was dyed in mummy which the skillful / Conserved of maiden's hearts.

It's true. There's magic woven into it. A prophetess who had lived two hundred years sewed it in a prophetic trance. The silkworms that made the silk were sacred, and it was dyed with fluid from mummified virgins' hearts.
Most veritable; therefore look to't well.
Absolutely true. So take good care of it.
Then would to God that I had never seen't!
Then I wish to God I'd never seen it!
Why do you speak so startingly and rash?
Why are you speaking so suddenly and sharply?
Is't lost? is't gone? speak, is it out o' the way?
Is it lost? Is it gone? Tell me, is it missing?
It is not lost; but what an if it were?
It isn't lost. But what if it were?
I say, it is not lost.
Get it. Let me see it.
Why, so I can, sir, but I will not now. / This is a trick to put me from my suit. / Pray you, let Cassio be received again.
Well, I could, sir, but I won't right now. This is a trick to distract me from my request. Please, take Cassio back.
Fetch me the handkerchief, my mind misgives.
Get me the handkerchief. I have a bad feeling.
Come, come, / You'll never meet a more sufficient man.
Come on, come on. You'll never find a more capable man.
I pray, talk me of Cassio.
Please, talk to me about Cassio.
A man that all his time / Hath founded his good fortunes on your love, / Shared dangers with you-
A man who has always based his success on your friendship, who shared dangers with you—
In sooth, you are to blame.
Honestly, you're the one in the wrong.
I ne'er saw this before. / Sure there's some wonder in this handkerchief; / I am most unhappy in the loss of it.
I never saw this before. There must be something magical about this handkerchief. I'm so unhappy that I've lost it.
'Tis not a year or two shows us a man. / They are all but stomachs and we all but food; / They eat us hungerly, and when they are full / They belch us. Look you! Cassio and my husband.
It doesn't take a year or two to show us what a man is. They're all just stomachs and we're just food. They eat us hungrily, and when they're full, they belch us up. Look! Cassio and my husband.
There is no other way; 'tis she must do't. / And, lo, the happiness! Go and importune her.
There's no other way. She's the one who has to do it. And look, what luck! Go and beg her.
How now, good Cassio! What's the news with you?
Hello, good Cassio! What's your news?

Madam, my former suit: I do beseech you / That by your virtuous means I may again / Exist and be a member of his love / Whom I with all the office of my heart / Entirely honor. I would not be delay'd. / If my offense be of such mortal kind / That nor my service past nor present sorrows / Nor purposed merit in futurity / Can ransom me into his love again, / But to know so must be my benefit; / So shall I clothe me in a forced content / And shut myself up in some other course / To Fortune's alms.

Madam, the same request as before. I beg you, through your good influence, let me live again and be a part of the love of the man I honor with all my heart. I don't want any delay. If my offense is so serious that neither my past service, nor my present sorrow, nor my promise of good service in the future can buy back his love, then just knowing that will be a benefit to me. Then I'll force myself to be content and take some other path, relying on Fortune's charity.

Alas, thrice-gentle Cassio! / My advocation is not now in tune; / My lord is not my lord, nor should I know him / Were he in favor as in humor alter'd. / So help me every spirit sanctified, / As I have spoken for you all my best / And stood within the blank of his displeasure / For my free speech! You must awhile be patient. / What I can do I will; and more I will / Than for myself I dare. Let that suffice you.

Alas, thrice-gentle Cassio! My pleading isn't working right now. My husband isn't himself. I wouldn't recognize him if his face had changed as much as his mood. So help me every holy spirit, I've spoken for you as well as I can and made myself the target of his anger for speaking so freely! You'll have to be patient for a while. What I can do, I will. And I'll do more for you than I'd dare to do for myself. Let that be enough for you.
He went hence but now, / And certainly in strange unquietness.
He just left, and he was certainly strangely upset.

Can he be angry? I have seen the cannon, / When it hath blown his ranks into the air / And, like the devil, from his very arm / Puff'd his own brother. And can he be angry? / Something of moment then. I will go meet him. / There's matter in't indeed if he be angry.

Can he be angry? I've seen the cannon blow his soldiers into the air and, like the devil, blast his own brother right out of his arms. And he's angry? It must be something important, then. I'll go find him. There's really something to it if he's angry.

Something sure of state, / Either from Venice or some unhatch'd practice / Made demonstrable here in Cyprus to him, / Hath puddled his clear spirit; and in such cases / Men's natures wrangle with inferior things, / Though great ones are their object. 'Tis even so; / For let our finger ache, and it indues / Our other healthful members even to that sense / Of pain. Nay, we must think men are not gods, / Nor of them look for such observancy / As fits the bridal. Beshrew me much, Emilia, / I was, unhandsome warrior as I am, / Arraigning his unkindness with my soul; / But now I find I had suborn'd the witness, / And he's indicted falsely.

It must be some state business, either news from Venice or some plot uncovered here in Cyprus, that has muddied his clear mind. In cases like that, men's tempers quarrel with small things even though big things are really on their minds. That's how it is. If our finger aches, the rest of our healthy body feels the pain too. No, we have to remember men aren't gods, and we can't expect them to be as attentive as on the wedding day. Scold me, Emilia: like the clumsy soldier I am, I was accusing him of unkindness in my heart. But now I realize I bribed the witness, and he's been falsely charged.
Pray heaven it be state matters, as you think, / And no conception nor no jealous toy / Concerning you.
Pray to heaven it's state business, as you think, and not some idea or jealous fancy about you.
Alas the day, I never gave him cause!
Oh no, I never gave him any reason!
But jealous souls will not be answer'd so; / They are not ever jealous for the cause, / But jealous for they are jealous. 'Tis a monster / Begot upon itself, born on itself.
But jealous people won't accept that answer. They're not jealous for a reason; they're jealous because they're jealous. It's a monster that conceives itself and gives birth to itself.
Heaven keep that monster from Othello's mind!
Heaven keep that monster away from Othello's mind!
I will go seek him. Cassio, walk hereabout. / If I do find him fit, I'll move your suit, / And seek to effect it to my uttermost.
I'll go look for him. Cassio, stay around here. If I find him in the right mood, I'll bring up your request and do my very best to make it happen.
What make you from home? / How is it with you, my most fair Bianca? / I'faith, sweet love, I was coming to your house.
What are you doing away from home? How are you, my lovely Bianca? Honestly, sweet love, I was coming to your house.

And I was going to your lodging, Cassio. / What, keep a week away? seven days and nights? / Eight score eight hours? and lovers' absent hours, / More tedious than the dial eight score times? / O weary reckoning!

And I was going to your place, Cassio. What, stay away for a week? Seven days and nights? A hundred and sixty-eight hours? And lovers' hours apart are a hundred and sixty times longer than clock hours. Oh, what a tiring count!
Pardon me, Bianca. / I have this while with leaden thoughts been press'd; / But I shall in a more continuate time / Strike off this score of absence. Sweet Bianca,
Forgive me, Bianca. I've been weighed down with heavy thoughts lately. But when I have more uninterrupted time, I'll pay off this debt of absence. Sweet Bianca,
O Cassio, whence came this? / This is some token from a newer friend. / To the felt absence now I feel a cause. / Is't come to this? Well, well.
Oh, Cassio, where did this come from? This is a gift from some new girlfriend. Now I know the reason for your absence. Has it come to this? Well, well.
Go to, woman! / Throw your vile guesses in the devil's teeth, / From whence you have them. You are jealous now / That this is from some mistress, some remembrance. / No, by my faith, Bianca.
Come on, woman! Throw your nasty guesses back in the devil's teeth, where you got them from. Now you're jealous that this is from some mistress, some keepsake. No, I swear, Bianca.
I know not, sweet. I found it in my chamber. / I like the work well. Ere it be demanded- / As like enough it will- I'ld have it copied. / Take it, and do't; and leave me for this time.

I don't know, sweetheart. I found it in my room. I like the embroidery. Before someone asks for it back (which they probably will), I'd like to have it copied. Take it and do it, and leave me for now.
I do attend here on the general; / And think it no addition, nor my wish, / To have him see me woman'd.
I'm waiting here for the general, and I don't think it would help me, nor do I want, to have him see me with a woman.
Not that I love you not.
Not that I don't love you.
But that you do not love me. / I pray you, bring me on the way a little, / And say if I shall see you soon at night.
But that you don't love me. Please, walk me part of the way, and tell me if I'll see you tonight.
'Tis but a little way that I can bring you, / For I attend here, but I'll see you soon.
I can only walk you a little way, because I have to wait here. But I'll see you soon.
'Tis very good; I must be circumstanced.
That's fine. I'll have to accept the circumstances.
Or to be naked with her friend in bed / An hour or more, not meaning any harm?
Or to be naked in bed with her friend for an hour or more, without meaning any harm?
Naked in bed, Iago, and not mean harm! / It is hypocrisy against the devil. / They that mean virtuously and yet do so, / The devil their virtue tempts and they tempt heaven.
Naked in bed, Iago, and not mean any harm! That's hypocrisy aimed at the devil. People who mean well and still do that are having their virtue tempted by the devil, and they're tempting heaven.
So they do nothing, 'tis a venial slip. / But if I give my wife a handkerchief-
If they don't do anything, it's a minor slip. But if I give my wife a handkerchief—
Why, then, 'tis hers, my lord, and being hers, / She may, I think, bestow't on any man.
Why, then it's hers, my lord. And since it's hers, I think she can give it to any man she wants.
She is protectress of her honor too. / May she give that?
She's the guardian of her honor too. Can she give that away?
Her honor is an essence that's not seen; / They have it very oft that have it not. / But for the handkerchief-
Her honor is something you can't see. Plenty of women seem to have it who don't. But as for the handkerchief—
By heaven, I would most gladly have forgot it. / Thou said'st- O, it comes o'er my memory, / As doth the raven o'er the infected house, / Boding to all- he had my handkerchief.
By heaven, I'd gladly have forgotten it. You said (oh, it hangs over my memory like a raven over a plague-stricken house, a bad omen for everyone) that he had my handkerchief.
That doesn't look so good now.

What, / If I had said I had seen him do you wrong? / Or heard him say- as knaves be such abroad, / Who having, by their own importunate suit, / Or voluntary dotage of some mistress, / Convinced or supplied them, cannot choose / But they must blab-

What if I'd said I'd seen him wrong you? Or heard him say... There are scoundrels out there who, once they've seduced a woman by their own persistent pleading or because she willingly fell for them, can't help bragging about it—
He hath, my lord; but be you well assured, / No more than he'll unswear.
He has, my lord. But rest assured, nothing more than he'd deny under oath.
Faith, that he did- I know not what he did.
Well, that he did... I don't know what he did.
With her, on her, what you will.
With her, on her, whatever you like.

Lie with her! lie on her! We say lie on her, when they / belie her. Lie with her! 'Zounds, that's fulsome! Handkerchief- / confessions- handkerchief! To confess and be hanged for his labor- / first, to be hanged, and then to confess. I tremble at it. / Nature would not invest herself in such shadowing passion without / some instruction. It is not words that shakes me thus. Pish! / Noses, ears, and lips. Is't possible? Confess? Handkerchief? O / devil!

Lie with her! Lie on her! We say "lie on her" when people tell lies about her. Lie with her! Damn it, that's disgusting! Handkerchief... confessions... handkerchief! Let him confess and be hanged for it. No, first hang him, and then let him confess. I'm shaking. My body wouldn't be overcome by such dark passion if there weren't some truth to this. It isn't just words that shake me like this. Ugh! Noses, ears, and lips. Is it possible? Confess? Handkerchief? Oh, devil!
Work on, / My medicine, work! Thus credulous fools are caught, / And many worthy and chaste dames even thus, / All guiltless, meet reproach. What, ho! My lord! / My lord, I say! Othello!
Keep working, my medicine, keep working! This is how gullible fools are caught. And this is how many worthy, chaste women, completely innocent, get disgraced. Hey! My lord! My lord, I say! Othello!
My lord is fall'n into an epilepsy. / This is his second fit; he had one yesterday.
My lord has had an epileptic fit. This is his second one; he had one yesterday.

No, forbear; / The lethargy must have his quiet course. / If not, he foams at mouth, and by and by / Breaks out to savage madness. Look, he stirs. / Do you withdraw yourself a little while, / He will recover straight. When he is gone, / I would on great occasion speak with you.

No, don't. The fit has to run its course quietly. Otherwise he foams at the mouth and soon breaks out into savage madness. Look, he's moving. Step away for a little while. He'll recover soon. When he's gone, I need to talk to you about something important.
How is it, general? Have you not hurt your head?
How are you, general? Did you hurt your head?
I mock you? No, by heaven. / Would you would bear your fortune like a man!
Me, mock you? No, by heaven. I just wish you'd take your bad luck like a man!
A horned man's a monster and a beast.
A man with horns is a monster and a beast.
There's many a beast then in a populous city, / And many a civil monster.
Then there are a lot of beasts in a crowded city, and plenty of well-mannered monsters.

Good sir, be a man; / Think every bearded fellow that's but yoked / May draw with you. There's millions now alive / That nightly lie in those unproper beds / Which they dare swear peculiar. Your case is better. / O, 'tis the spite of hell, the fiend's arch-mock, / To lip a wanton in a secure couch, / And to suppose her chaste! No, let me know, / And knowing what I am, I know what she shall be.

Good sir, be a man. Think of every bearded man who's married: he's pulling the same cart you are. There are millions of men alive right now who go to bed every night in beds others have used, and they'd swear those beds were theirs alone. Your situation is better. Oh, it's hell's own spite, the devil's greatest joke, to kiss a slut in a bed you think is safe and believe she's chaste! No, I'd rather know. And knowing what I am, I know what she'll get.

Stand you awhile apart, / Confine yourself but in a patient list. / Whilst you were here o'erwhelmed with your grief- / A passion most unsuiting such a man- / Cassio came hither. I shifted him away, / And laid good 'scuse upon your ecstasy; / Bade him anon return and here speak with me / The which he promised. Do but encave yourself / And mark the fleers, the gibes, and notable scorns, / That dwell in every region of his face; / For I will make him tell the tale anew, / Where, how, how oft, how long ago, and when / He hath and is again to cope your wife. / I say, but mark his gesture. Marry, patience, / Or I shall say you are all in all in spleen, / And nothing of a man.

Stand aside for a while and keep yourself under control. While you were lying here overcome by your grief (a passion that doesn't suit a man like you), Cassio came by. I got rid of him and gave a good excuse for your fit. I told him to come back soon and talk to me here, which he promised to do. Just hide yourself and watch the sneers, the mockery, and the obvious contempt all over his face. Because I'll get him to tell the story again: where, how, how often, how long ago, and when he has slept with your wife and will again. Just watch his gestures, I say. But be patient, or I'll say you're nothing but temper and not a man at all.
Dost thou hear, Iago? / I will be found most cunning in my patience; / But (dost thou hear?) most bloody.
Do you hear me, Iago? I'll be very clever in my patience. But (do you hear?) very bloody.
That's not amiss; / But yet keep time in all. Will you withdraw?
That's fine, but keep control of yourself through all of it. Will you step back?

Now will I question Cassio of Bianca, / A housewife that by selling her desires / Buys herself bread and clothes. It is a creature / That dotes on Cassio, as 'tis the strumpet's plague / To beguile many and be beguiled by one. / He, when he hears of her, cannot refrain / From the excess of laughter. Here he comes.

Now I'll ask Cassio about Bianca, a woman who sells her body to buy herself bread and clothes. She's crazy about Cassio, since it's a whore's curse to fool many men and be fooled by one. When he hears her name, he can't help laughing his head off. Here he comes.
As he shall smile, Othello shall go mad; / And his unbookish jealousy must construe / Poor Cassio's smiles, gestures, and light behavior / Quite in the wrong. How do you now, lieutenant?
When he smiles, Othello will go mad. And his ignorant jealousy will completely misread poor Cassio's smiles, gestures, and lighthearted behavior. How are you now, lieutenant?
The worser that you give me the addition / Whose want even kills me.
Worse, since you call me by the title whose loss is killing me.
Ply Desdemona well, and you are sure on't. / Now, if this suit lay in Bianco's power, / How quickly should you speed!
Keep working on Desdemona, and you'll get it for sure. Now, if this request were up to Bianca, how quickly you'd succeed!
I never knew a woman love man so.
I never knew a woman to love a man so much.
Alas, poor rogue! I think, i'faith, she loves me.
Oh, poor thing! I really think she does love me.
Now he denies it faintly and laughs it out.
Now he weakly denies it and laughs it off.
Now he importunes him / To tell it o'er. Go to; well said, well said.
Now Iago's urging him to tell it again. Go on. Well done, well done.
She gives it out that you shall marry her. / Do you intend it?
She's telling everyone you're going to marry her. Do you intend to?
Do you triumph, Roman? Do you triumph?
Are you gloating, like a Roman conqueror? Are you gloating?
I marry her! What? A customer! I prithee, bear some charity / to my wit; do not think it so unwholesome. Ha, ha, ha!
Me, marry her? What? A prostitute? Please, give my judgment some credit. Don't think I'm that far gone. Ha, ha, ha!
So, so, so, so. They laugh that win.
So, so, so, so. The winner gets to laugh.
Faith, the cry goes that you shall marry her.
Honestly, the word is that you'll marry her.
I am a very villain else.
I'm a complete villain if I'm not.
Have you marked me as a cuckold? Fine.
This is the monkey's own giving out. She is persuaded I / will marry her, out of her own love and flattery, not out of my / promise.
This is the monkey's own story. She's convinced I'll marry her because she loves me and flatters herself, not because I promised.
Iago beckons me; now he begins the story.
Iago's signaling to me. Now he's starting the story.

She was here even now; she haunts me in every place. I was / the other day talking on the sea bank with certain Venetians, and / thither comes the bauble, and, by this hand, she falls me thus / about my neck-

She was here just now. She follows me everywhere. The other day I was talking with some Venetians on the beach, and along comes the silly thing, and I swear, she throws her arms around my neck like this—
Crying, "O dear Cassio!" as it were; his gesture imports / it.
Crying, "Oh, dear Cassio!" or something like that. His gestures show it.
So hangs and lolls and weeps upon me; so hales and pulls / me. Ha, ha, ha!
She hangs on me and drapes herself over me and cries on me, and tugs and pulls at me. Ha, ha, ha!
Now he tells how she plucked him to my chamber. O, I see / that nose of yours, but not that dog I shall throw it to.
Now he's telling how she dragged him to my bedroom. Oh, I see that nose of yours, but not the dog I'll throw it to.
Well, I must leave her company.
Well, I have to stop seeing her.
Before me! look where she comes.
'Tis such another fitchew! marry, a perfumed one.
She's a real polecat! A perfumed one, though.
What do you mean by this haunting of me?
What do you mean by following me around like this?

Let the devil and his dam haunt you! What did you mean by / that same handkerchief you gave me even now? I was a fine fool to / take it. I must take out the work? A likely piece of work that / you should find it in your chamber and not know who left it / there! This is some minx's token, and I must take out the work? / There, give it your hobbyhorse. Wheresoever you had it, I'll take / out no work on't.

Let the devil and his mother follow you around! What did you mean by that handkerchief you just gave me? I was a real fool to take it. I'm supposed to copy the embroidery? A likely story, that you found it in your room and don't know who left it there! This is a present from some slut, and I'm supposed to copy it? Here, give it to your little whore. Wherever you got it, I won't copy any of it.
How now, my sweet Bianca! how now! how now!
What's this, my sweet Bianca? What's going on? What's the matter?
By heaven, that should be my handkerchief!
By heaven, that must be my handkerchief!
An you'll come to supper tonight, you may; an you will not, / come when you are next prepared for.
If you want to come to supper tonight, you can. If you don't, come whenever you're next invited, which will be never.
Go after her, go after her.
Faith, I must; she'll rail i' the street else.
Honestly, I have to. Otherwise she'll scream at me in the street.
Well, I may chance to see you, for I would very fain speak / with you.
Well, I might see you there, because I really need to talk to you.
[Advancing.] How shall I murther him, Iago?
[Coming forward.] How should I kill him, Iago?
Did you perceive how he laughed at his vice?
Did you see how he laughed about his sin?
And did you see the handkerchief?
And did you see the handkerchief?
Yours, by this hand. And to see how he prizes the foolish / woman your wife! She gave it him, and he hath given it his whore.
Yours, I swear. And look how little he values your foolish wife! She gave it to him, and he gave it to his whore.
I would have him nine years akilling. A fine woman! a fair / woman! a sweet woman!
I want to spend nine years killing him. A fine woman! A beautiful woman! A sweet woman!
No, you have to forget that.

Ay, let her rot, and perish, and be damned tonight, for / she shall not live. No, my heart is turned to stone; I strike it, / and it hurts my hand. O, the world hath not a sweeter creature. / She might lie by an emperor's side, and command him tasks.

Yes, let her rot and perish and be damned tonight, because she won't live. No, my heart has turned to stone. I hit it, and it hurts my hand. Oh, the world has no sweeter creature. She could lie beside an emperor and give him orders.
No, that's not the way to think.
Hang her! I do but say what she is. So delicate with her / needle, an admirable musician. O, she will sing the savageness / out of a bear. Of so high and plenteous wit and invention-
Hang her! I'm only saying what she is. So skillful with her needle, a wonderful musician. Oh, her singing could tame a savage bear. So intelligent and imaginative—
She's the worse for all this.
She's all the worse for all this.
O, a thousand, a thousand times. And then, of so gentle a / condition!
Oh, a thousand, a thousand times worse. And she has such a gentle nature!
Yes, too gentle, too easily yielding.
Nay, that's certain. But yet the pity of it, Iago! / O Iago, the pity of it, Iago!
No, that's certain. But still, the pity of it, Iago! Oh, Iago, the pity of it, Iago!
If you are so fond over her iniquity, give her patent to / offend, for, if it touch not you, it comes near nobody.
If you're so fond of her sins, give her a license to sin. Because if it doesn't bother you, it doesn't bother anyone.
I will chop her into messes. Cuckold me!
I'll chop her into little pieces. Make me a cuckold!
Get me some poison, Iago, this night. I'll not expostulate / with her, lest her body and beauty unprovide my mind again. This / night, Iago.
Get me some poison tonight, Iago. I won't argue with her, in case her body and beauty weaken my resolve again. Tonight, Iago.
Do it not with poison, strangle her in her bed, even the bed / she hath contaminated.
Don't use poison. Strangle her in her bed, the very bed she has contaminated.
Good, good, the justice of it pleases, very good.
Good, good. I like the justice of it. Very good.
And for Cassio, let me be his undertaker. You shall hear more / by midnight.
And as for Cassio, let me take care of him. You'll hear more by midnight.
Excellent good. [A trumpet within.] What trumpet is that / same?
Excellent. [A trumpet offstage.] What's that trumpet?
Something from Venice, sure. 'Tis Lodovico / Come from the Duke. And, see your wife is with him.
Something from Venice, I'm sure. It's Lodovico, sent by the Duke. And look, your wife is with him.
The Duke and Senators of Venice greet you.
The Duke and Senators of Venice send their greetings.
I kiss the instrument of their pleasures.
I kiss this document of their orders.
And what's the news, good cousin Lodovico?
And what's the news, good cousin Lodovico?
I am very glad to see you, signior; / Welcome to Cyprus.
I'm very glad to see you, sir. Welcome to Cyprus.
I thank you. How does Lieutenant Cassio?
Thank you. How is Lieutenant Cassio?
Cousin, there's fall'n between him and my lord / An unkind breech; but you shall make all well.
Cousin, there's been an unfortunate falling-out between him and my husband. But you'll make everything right.
[Reads.] "This fail you not to do, as you will-"
[Reading.] "Do not fail to do this, as you will—"
He did not call; he's busy in the paper. / Is there division 'twixt my lord and Cassio?
He wasn't talking to you; he's busy with the letter. Is there a quarrel between my lord and Cassio?
A most unhappy one. I would do much / To atone them, for the love I bear to Cassio.
A very unhappy one. I'd do a lot to reconcile them, because of the affection I have for Cassio.
Are you in your right mind?
May be the letter moved him; / For, as I think, they do command him home, / Deputing Cassio in his government.
Maybe the letter upset him. As I understand it, they're ordering him home and putting Cassio in charge here in his place.
By my troth, I am glad on't.
I am glad to see you mad.
I'm glad to see you've lost your mind.
My lord, this would not be believed in Venice, / Though I should swear I saw't. 'Tis very much. / Make her amends; she weeps.
My lord, no one in Venice would believe this, even if I swore I saw it. This is too much. Apologize to her. She's crying.
O devil, devil! / If that the earth could teem with woman's tears, / Each drop she falls would prove a crocodile. / Out of my sight!
Oh, devil, devil! If the earth could be made pregnant by women's tears, every tear she drops would turn into a crocodile. Get out of my sight!
[Going.] I will not stay to offend you.
[Going.] I won't stay and offend you.
Truly, an obedient lady. / I do beseech your lordship, call her back.
Truly, an obedient lady. I beg you, my lord, call her back.
What would you with her, sir?
What do you want with her, sir?

Ay, you did wish that I would make her turn. / Sir, she can turn and turn, and yet go on, / And turn again; and she can weep, sir, weep; / And she's obedient, as you say, obedient, / Very obedient. Proceed you in your tears. / Concerning this, sir- O well-painted passion!- / I am commanded home. Get you away; / I'll send for you anon. Sir, I obey the mandate, / And will return to Venice. Hence, avaunt!

Yes, you wanted me to make her turn around. Sir, she can turn and turn, and still keep going, and turn again. And she can cry, sir, cry. And she's obedient, as you say, obedient, very obedient. Go on with your tears. About this letter, sir... Oh, what a well-acted show of grief! I'm ordered home. Get out of here; I'll send for you soon. Sir, I'll obey the order and return to Venice. Go, get out!
Cassio shall have my place. And, sir, tonight, / I do entreat that we may sup together. / You are welcome, sir, to Cyprus. Goats and monkeys!
Cassio will take over my position. And, sir, I invite you to have supper with me tonight. Welcome to Cyprus, sir. Goats and monkeys!

Is this the noble Moor whom our full Senate / Call all in all sufficient? This the nature / Whom passion could not shake? whose solid virtue / The shot of accident nor dart of chance / Could neither graze nor pierce?

Is this the noble Moor whom our whole Senate calls completely capable? Is this the man whom passion couldn't shake, whose solid virtue couldn't be grazed or pierced by the bullets of accident or the arrows of chance?
Are his wits safe? Is he not light of brain?
Is he in his right mind? Has he gone mad?
He's that he is. I may not breathe my censure / What he might be: if what he might he is not, / I would to heaven he were!
He is what he is. It's not my place to say what he might be. If he isn't what he should be, I wish to heaven he were!
Faith, that was not so well; yet would I knew / That stroke would prove the worst!
Honestly, that wasn't good. But I wish I knew that blow would be the worst of it!
Is it his use? / Or did the letters work upon his blood, / And new create this fault?
Is this his habit? Or did the letters stir up his temper and create this fault?

Alas, alas! / It is not honesty in me to speak / What I have seen and known. You shall observe him, / And his own courses will denote him so / That I may save my speech. Do but go after, / And mark how he continues.

Alas, alas! It wouldn't be honest of me to tell you what I've seen and known. You watch him, and his own actions will show you what he is, so I won't have to say anything. Just follow him and see how he goes on.
I am sorry that I am deceived in him.
I'm sorry I was so wrong about him.
Nor ever heard, nor ever did suspect.
Nor heard anything, nor ever suspected anything.
Yes, you have seen Cassio and she together.
Yes, you've seen Cassio and her together.
But then I saw no harm, and then I heard / Each syllable that breath made up between them.
But I didn't see anything wrong, and I heard every syllable they said to each other.
Nor send you out o' the way?
To fetch her fan, her gloves, her mask, nor nothing?
To get her fan, her gloves, her mask, or anything?

I durst, my lord, to wager she is honest, / Lay down my soul at stake. If you think other, / Remove your thought; it doth abuse your bosom. / If any wretch have put this in your head, / Let heaven requite it with the serpent's curse! / For if she be not honest, chaste, and true, / There's no man happy; the purest of their wives / Is foul as slander.

My lord, I'd bet my soul that she's faithful. If you think otherwise, get rid of the thought; it's poisoning your heart. If some wretch has put this into your head, let heaven punish him with the curse it gave the serpent! Because if she isn't honest, chaste, and true, no husband is happy; the purest wife is as foul as slander.
Tell her to come here. Go.
She says enough; yet she's a simple bawd / That cannot say as much. This is a subtle whore, / A closet lock and key of villainous secrets. / And yet she'll kneel and pray; I have seen her do't.

She says enough. But any brothel-keeper who couldn't say as much would be a simple one. This woman's a clever whore, a locked cabinet full of wicked secrets. And yet she'll kneel and pray; I've seen her do it.
My lord, what is your will?
My lord, what do you want?
Let me see your eyes; / Look in my face.
Let me see your eyes. Look at my face.
[To Emilia.] Some of your function, mistress, / Leave procreants alone and shut the door; / Cough, or cry "hem," if anybody come. / Your mystery, your mystery; nay, dispatch.
[To Emilia.] Do your job, madam. Leave the lovers alone and shut the door. Cough or say "ahem" if anyone comes. Your trade, your trade! Go on, hurry.
Upon my knees, what doth your speech import? / I understand a fury in your words, / But not the words.
I beg you on my knees, what do your words mean? I can hear the fury in them, but I don't understand the words.
Your wife, my lord, your true and loyal wife.
Your wife, my lord, your true and loyal wife.
Come, swear it, damn thyself; / Lest, being like one of heaven, the devils themselves / Should fear to seize thee. Therefore be double-damn'd; / Swear thou art honest.
Come on, swear it, and damn yourself. Because you look like an angel, the devils themselves might be afraid to grab you. So be doubly damned: swear you're faithful.
Heaven truly knows that thou art false as hell.
Heaven truly knows you're as false as hell.
To whom, my lord? with whom? how am I false?
False to whom, my lord? With whom? How am I false?

Alas the heavy day! Why do you weep? / Am I the motive of these tears, my lord? / If haply you my father do suspect / An instrument of this your calling back, / Lay not your blame on me. If you have lost him, / Why, I have lost him too.

Oh, what a terrible day! Why are you crying? Am I the reason for these tears, my lord? If you suspect my father had a hand in your being called home, don't blame me. If you've lost his friendship, well, I've lost him too.

Had it pleased heaven / To try me with affliction, had they rain'd / All kinds of sores and shames on my bare head, / Steep'd me in poverty to the very lips, / Given to captivity me and my utmost hopes, / I should have found in some place of my soul / A drop of patience; but, alas, to make me / A fixed figure for the time of scorn / To point his slow unmoving finger at! / Yet could I bear that too, well, very well; / But there, where I have garner'd up my heart, / Where either I must live or bear no life; / The fountain from the which my current runs, / Or else dries up; to be discarded thence! / Or keep it as a cistern for foul toads / To knot and gender in! Turn thy complexion there, / Patience, thou young and rose-lipp'd cherubin, / Ay, there, look grim as hell!

If heaven had wanted to test me with suffering, if it had rained every kind of sore and shame on my bare head, drowned me in poverty up to my lips, made a prisoner of me and all my highest hopes, I'd have found somewhere in my soul a drop of patience. But, alas, to make me a fixed target for the scornful world to point its slow, unmoving finger at! Still, I could bear that too, well, very well. But there, where I've stored up my heart, where I must either live or not live at all, the spring my life flows from or else dries up: to be thrown out of there! Or to have to keep it as a tank where filthy toads tangle and breed! Change color at that, Patience, you young, rosy-lipped angel. Yes, at that, look as grim as hell!
I hope my noble lord esteems me honest.
I hope my noble lord thinks I'm faithful.

O, ay, as summer flies are in the shambles, / That quicken even with blowing. O thou weed, / Who art so lovely fair and smell'st so sweet / That the sense aches at thee, would thou hadst ne'er been born!

Oh, yes, as faithful as summer flies in a slaughterhouse, which breed again the moment their eggs are laid. Oh, you weed, who are so lovely and beautiful and smell so sweet that it makes the senses ache, I wish you'd never been born!
Alas, what ignorant sin have I committed?
Alas, what sin have I committed without knowing it?

Was this fair paper, this most goodly book, / Made to write "whore" upon? What committed? / Committed? O thou public commoner! / I should make very forges of my cheeks, / That would to cinders burn up modesty, / Did I but speak thy deeds. What committed! / Heaven stops the nose at it, and the moon winks; / The bawdy wind, that kisses all it meets, / Is hush'd within the hollow mine of earth, / And will not hear it. What committed? / Impudent strumpet!

Was this beautiful paper, this lovely book, made to have "whore" written on it? Committed? What have you committed? Oh, you common prostitute! If I just named what you've done, my cheeks would burn like furnaces and turn modesty to ashes. What have you committed! Heaven holds its nose at it, and the moon shuts its eyes. The promiscuous wind, which kisses everything it meets, hides in the hollow caves of the earth and won't listen to it. What have you committed? Shameless whore!
By heaven, you do me wrong.
No, as I am a Christian. / If to preserve this vessel for my lord / From any other foul unlawful touch / Be not to be a strumpet, I am none.
No, as I'm a Christian. If keeping this body for my husband alone, away from any other foul, unlawful touch, means I'm not a whore, then I'm not one.
No, as I shall be saved.
No, as I hope to be saved.

I cry you mercy then; / I took you for that cunning whore of Venice / That married with Othello. [Raises his voice.] You, mistress, / That have the office opposite to Saint Peter, / And keep the gate of hell!
Then I beg your pardon. I mistook you for that cunning whore of Venice who married Othello. [Raising his voice.] You, madam, whose job is the opposite of Saint Peter's, guarding the gate of hell!
You, you, ay, you! / We have done our course; there's money for your pains. / I pray you, turn the key, and keep our counsel.
You, you, yes, you! We're finished. Here's money for your trouble. Please, turn the key and keep our secret.
Alas, what does this gentleman conceive? / How do you, madam? How do you, my good lady?
Oh, what is this gentleman imagining? How are you, madam? How are you, my good lady?
Good madam, what's the matter with my lord?
Good madam, what's the matter with my lord?
He that is yours, sweet lady.
The one who's yours, sweet lady.

I have none. Do not talk to me, Emilia; / I cannot weep, nor answer have I none / But what should go by water. Prithee, tonight / Lay on my bed my wedding sheets. Remember, / And call thy husband hither.
I have none. Don't talk to me, Emilia. I can't cry, and I have no answers except tears. Please, tonight, put my wedding sheets on my bed. Remember. And call your husband here.
'Tis meet I should be used so, very meet. / How have I been behaved, that he might stick / The small'st opinion on my least misuse?
It's right that I should be treated like this, very right. How have I behaved that he could attach even the slightest suspicion to my smallest fault?
What is your pleasure, madam? How is't with you?
What can I do for you, madam? How are you?
I cannot tell. Those that do teach young babes / Do it with gentle means and easy tasks. / He might have chid me so, for in good faith, / I am a child to chiding.
I don't know. People who teach young children do it gently and with easy tasks. He could have scolded me that way, because honestly, I'm a child when it comes to being scolded.
Alas, Iago, my lord hath so bewhored her, / Thrown such despite and heavy terms upon her, / As true hearts cannot bear.
Oh, Iago, my lord has called her a whore and heaped such abuse and harsh words on her that no true heart could bear it.
Such as she says my lord did say I was.
The one she says my lord called me.
He call'd her whore; a beggar in his drink / Could not have laid such terms upon his callet.
He called her a whore. A drunken beggar couldn't have called his trashy girlfriend worse names.
I do not know; I am sure I am none such.
I don't know. I'm sure I'm not one.
Do not weep, do not weep. Alas the day!
Don't cry, don't cry. What a terrible day!
Hath she forsook so many noble matches, / Her father and her country and her friends, / To be call'd whore? Would it not make one weep?
Did she give up so many noble marriage offers, her father, her country, and her friends, to be called a whore? Wouldn't that make anyone cry?
Beshrew him for't! / How comes this trick upon him?
Curse him for it! How did he get this idea?
I will be hang'd, if some eternal villain, / Some busy and insinuating rogue, / Some cogging, cozening slave, to get some office, / Have not devised this slander; I'll be hang'd else.
I'll be hanged if some damned villain, some meddling, scheming scoundrel, some lying, cheating slave, didn't invent this slander to get himself some promotion. I'll be hanged if it isn't so.
Fie, there is no such man; it is impossible.
Come on, there's no such man. It's impossible.
If any such there be, heaven pardon him!
If there is, may heaven forgive him!

A halter pardon him! And hell gnaw his bones! / Why should he call her whore? Who keeps her company? / What place? What time? What form? What likelihood? / The Moor's abused by some most villainous knave, / Some base notorious knave, some scurvy fellow. / O heaven, that such companions thou'ldst unfold, / And put in every honest hand a whip / To lash the rascals naked through the world / Even from the east to the west!

May a noose forgive him! And may hell gnaw his bones! Why would he call her a whore? Who has she been with? Where? When? How? What's the evidence? The Moor's been tricked by some vicious villain, some low, notorious villain, some scummy creep. Oh heaven, I wish you'd expose such men and put a whip in every honest hand to lash those rascals naked across the world, from east to west!
O, fie upon them! Some such squire he was / That turn'd your wit the seamy side without, / And made you to suspect me with the Moor.
Oh, to hell with them! It was a guy like that who turned your brain inside out and made you suspect me with the Moor.
You are a fool; go to.

O good Iago, / What shall I do to win my lord again? / Good friend, go to him, for by this light of heaven, / I know not how I lost him. Here I kneel: / If e'er my will did trespass 'gainst his love / Either in discourse of thought or actual deed, / Or that mine eyes, mine ears, or any sense, / Delighted them in any other form, / Or that I do not yet, and ever did, / And ever will, though he do shake me off / To beggarly divorcement, love him dearly, / Comfort forswear me! Unkindness may do much, / And his unkindness may defeat my life, / But never taint my love. I cannot say "whore." / It doth abhor me now I speak the word; / To do the act that might the addition earn / Not the world's mass of vanity could make me.

Oh, good Iago, what should I do to win my husband back? Good friend, go to him, because by the light of heaven, I don't know how I lost him. Here I kneel. If my heart ever betrayed his love, either in thought or in action, or if my eyes, my ears, or any of my senses ever took pleasure in any other man, or if I don't still love him dearly, and always did, and always will, even if he throws me off into a beggarly divorce, may I never know comfort again! Unkindness can do a lot, and his unkindness may destroy my life, but it will never spoil my love. I can't say "whore." It disgusts me just to say the word. Not all the riches in the world could make me do what would earn that name.
I pray you, be content; 'tis but his humor: / The business of the state does him offense, / And he does chide with you.
Please, calm down. It's just his mood. Government business is upsetting him, and he's taking it out on you.
'Tis but so, I warrant. [Trumpets within.] / Hark, how these instruments summon to supper! / The messengers of Venice stay the meat. / Go in, and weep not; all things shall be well.
That's all it is, I promise. [Trumpets offstage.] Listen, those trumpets are calling everyone to supper! The messengers from Venice are waiting to eat. Go in, and don't cry. Everything will be fine.
I do not find that thou dealest justly with me.
I don't think you're dealing fairly with me.

Every day thou daffest me with some device, Iago; and / rather, as it seems to me now, keepest from me all conveniency / than suppliest me with the least advantage of hope. I will indeed / no longer endure it; nor am I yet persuaded to put up in peace / what already I have foolishly suffered.

Every day you put me off with some trick, Iago. And now it seems to me you're keeping me from any opportunity rather than giving me even the slightest hope. I really won't put up with it anymore. And I'm not ready to quietly accept what I've already foolishly suffered.
Will you listen to me, Roderigo?
Faith, I have heard too much, for your words and / performances are no kin together.
Honestly, I've listened too much already, because your words and your actions have nothing to do with each other.

With nought but truth. I have wasted myself out of my / means. The jewels you have had from me to deliver to Desdemona / would half have corrupted a votarist. You have told me she hath / received them and returned me expectations and comforts of sudden / respect and acquaintance; but I find none.

It's nothing but the truth. I've spent everything I had. The jewels you got from me to give to Desdemona would have half corrupted a nun. You told me she'd received them and sent back hopes and promises of special attention and getting to know me soon. But I haven't seen any of that.
Very well! go to! I cannot go to, man; nor 'tis not very / well. By this hand, I say 'tis very scurvy, and begin to find / myself fopped in it.
Very well! Go on! I can't go on, man, and it's not very well. I swear, I say it's very rotten, and I'm beginning to realize I've been made a fool of.

I tell you 'tis not very well. I will make myself known / to Desdemona. If she will return me my jewels, I will give over / my suit and repent my unlawful solicitation; if not, assure / yourself I will seek satisfaction of you.

I'm telling you it's not very well. I'm going to make myself known to Desdemona. If she'll give me back my jewels, I'll give up my courtship and repent of my unlawful pursuit. If not, you can be sure I'll demand satisfaction from you.
Ay, and said nothing but what I protest intendment of / doing.
Yes, and I've said nothing I don't fully intend to do.

Why, now I see there's mettle in thee; and even from this / instant do build on thee a better opinion than ever before. Give / me thy hand, Roderigo. Thou hast taken against me a most just / exception; but yet, I protest, have dealt most directly in thy / affair.

Why, now I see there's some backbone in you. And from this moment on I think more of you than ever before. Give me your hand, Roderigo. You've raised a very fair objection against me. But I swear, I've dealt with your business very honestly.

I grant indeed it hath not appeared, and your suspicion is / not without wit and judgement. But, Roderigo, if thou hast that / in thee indeed, which I have greater reason to believe now than / ever, I mean purpose, courage, and valor, this night show it; if / thou the next night following enjoy not Desdemona, take me from / this world with treachery and devise engines for my life.

I admit it hasn't looked like it, and your suspicion shows some intelligence and judgment. But, Roderigo, if you really have in you what I now have more reason than ever to believe (I mean determination, courage, and bravery), show it tonight. If you don't enjoy Desdemona the following night, then kill me by treachery and plot against my life.
Well, what is it? Is it within reason and compass?
Well, what is it? Is it reasonable and possible?
Sir, there is especial commission come from Venice to depute / Cassio in Othello's place.
Sir, a special order has come from Venice to put Cassio in Othello's place.
Is that true? Why then Othello and Desdemona return again / to Venice.
Is that true? Then Othello and Desdemona will go back to Venice.
O, no; he goes into Mauritania, and takes away with him the / fair Desdemona, unless his abode be lingered here by some / accident; wherein none can be so determinate as the removing of / Cassio.
Oh, no. He's going to Mauritania and taking the beautiful Desdemona with him, unless something happens to keep him here. And nothing could do that more decisively than removing Cassio.
How do you mean, removing of him?
What do you mean, removing him?
Why, by making him uncapable of Othello's place; knocking out / his brains.
Why, by making him unable to take Othello's place: knocking his brains out.
And that you would have me to do?
And you want me to do that?

Ay, if you dare do yourself a profit and a right. He sups / tonight with a harlotry, and thither will I go to him. He knows / not yet of his honorable fortune. If you will watch his going / thence, which his will fashion to fall out between twelve and / one, you may take him at your pleasure; I will be near to second / your attempt, and he shall fall between us. Come, stand not / amazed at it, but go along with me; I will show you such a / necessity in his death that you shall think yourself bound to put / it on him. It is now high supper-time, and the night grows to / waste. About it.

Yes, if you dare to do yourself some good and get what you deserve. He's having supper tonight with a whore, and I'll meet him there. He doesn't know about his promotion yet. If you watch for him leaving, which I'll arrange to happen between twelve and one, you can attack him however you like. I'll be nearby to back you up, and between us he'll go down. Come on, don't stand there stunned. Come with me. I'll show you why his death is so necessary that you'll feel obligated to kill him. It's well past supper time, and the night's wasting away. Let's get to it.
I will hear further reason for this.
I want to hear more reasons for this.
And you will, to your satisfaction.
I do beseech you, sir, trouble yourself no further.
Please, sir, don't trouble yourself any further.
O, pardon me; 'twill do me good to walk.
Oh, excuse me. It'll do me good to walk.
Madam, good night; I humbly thank your ladyship.
Good night, madam. I humbly thank your ladyship.
Will you walk, sir? / O- Desdemona-
Shall we walk, sir? Oh, Desdemona—
Get you to bed on the instant; I will be returned / forthwith. Dismiss your attendant there; look it be done.
Go to bed right away. I'll be back soon. Send your attendant away. Make sure it's done.
How goes it now? He looks gentler than he did.
How are things now? He looks gentler than he did.
He says he will return incontinent. / He hath commanded me to go to bed, / And bade me to dismiss you.
He says he'll be back right away. He's ordered me to go to bed and told me to send you away.
It was his bidding; therefore, good Emilia, / Give me my nightly wearing, and adieu. / We must not now displease him.
Those were his orders. So, good Emilia, give me my nightclothes, and goodbye. We mustn't upset him now.
I would you had never seen him!
I wish you'd never seen him!
So would not I. My love doth so approve him, / That even his stubbornness, his checks, his frowns- / Prithee, unpin me- have grace and favor in them.
I don't. I love him so much that even his stubbornness, his scolding, his frowns (please, unpin me) have a grace and charm to them.
I have laid those sheets you bade me on the bed.
I've put those sheets you asked for on the bed.
All's one. Good faith, how foolish are our minds! / If I do die before thee, prithee shroud me / In one of those same sheets.
It doesn't matter. Honestly, how foolish our minds are! If I die before you, please wrap me in one of those sheets.
Come on, come on, you're just talking.

My mother had a maid call'd Barbary; / She was in love, and he she loved proved mad / And did forsake her. She had a song of "willow"; / An old thing 'twas, but it express'd her fortune, / And she died singing it. That song tonight / Will not go from my mind; I have much to do / But to go hang my head all at one side / And sing it like poor Barbary. Prithee, dispatch.

My mother had a maid named Barbary. She was in love, and the man she loved went mad and left her. She had a song called "Willow." It was an old song, but it described her situation, and she died singing it. Tonight I can't get that song out of my head. It's all I can do not to hang my head to one side and sing it like poor Barbary. Please, hurry.
Shall I go fetch your nightgown?
Shall I go get your nightgown?
No, unpin me here. / This Lodovico is a proper man.
No, unpin me here. This Lodovico is a fine man.
I know a lady in Venice would have walked barefoot to / Palestine for a touch of his nether lip.
I know a lady in Venice who would have walked barefoot to Palestine for one touch of his lower lip.

[Sings.] / "The poor soul sat sighing by a sycamore tree, / Sing all a green willow; / Her hand on her bosom, her head on her knee, / Sing willow, willow, willow. / The fresh streams ran by her, and murmur'd her moans, / Sing willow, willow, willow; / Her salt tears fell from her, and soften'd the stones-" / Lay be these- / "Sing willow, willow, willow-" / Prithee, hie thee; he'll come anon- / "Sing all a green willow must be my garland. / Let nobody blame him; his scorn I approve-" / Nay, that's not next. Hark, who is't that knocks?

[Singing.] "The poor soul sat sighing by a sycamore tree, sing all a green willow; her hand on her chest, her head on her knee, sing willow, willow, willow. The fresh streams ran by her and murmured her moans, sing willow, willow, willow; her salt tears fell from her and softened the stones." Put these away. "Sing willow, willow, willow." Please, hurry; he'll be here soon. "Sing all a green willow must be my garland. Let nobody blame him; I accept his scorn." No, that's not the next line. Listen, who's knocking?

[Sings.] / "I call'd my love false love; but what said he then? / Sing willow, willow, willow. / If I court moe women, you'll couch with moe men-" / So get thee gone; good night. Mine eyes do itch; / Doth that bode weeping?

[Singing.] "I called my love false love; but what did he say then? Sing willow, willow, willow. If I court more women, you'll sleep with more men." So go now. Good night. My eyes itch. Does that mean I'll cry?
I have heard it said so. O, these men, these men! / Dost thou in conscience think- tell me, Emilia- / That there be women do abuse their husbands / In such gross kind?
I've heard it said that it does. Oh, these men, these men! Do you honestly think (tell me, Emilia) that there are women who cheat on their husbands so grossly?
There be some such, no question.
There are some, no doubt about it.
Wouldst thou do such a deed for all the world?
Would you do such a thing for the whole world?
Nor I neither by this heavenly light; I might do't as well / i' the dark.
Neither would I, by this heavenly light. I'd rather do it in the dark.
Wouldst thou do such a deed for all the world?
Would you do such a thing for the whole world?
The world's a huge thing; it is a great price / For a small vice.
The world's a huge thing. It's a big reward for a small sin.
In troth, I think thou wouldst not.
Honestly, I don't think you would.

In troth, I think I should, and undo't when I had done. / Marry, I would not do such a thing for a joint-ring, nor for / measures of lawn, nor for gowns, petticoats, nor caps, nor any / petty exhibition; but, for the whole world- why, who would not / make her husband a cuckold to make him a monarch? I should / venture purgatory for't.

Honestly, I think I would, and undo it once I'd done it. Of course, I wouldn't do it for a cheap ring, or for some fine linen, or for dresses, petticoats, hats, or any little gift. But for the whole world? Why, who wouldn't cheat on her husband to make him a king? I'd risk purgatory for that.
Beshrew me, if I would do such a wrong / For the whole world.
Damn me if I'd do such a wrong for the whole world.
Why, the wrong is but a wrong i' the world; and having the / world for your labor, 'tis a wrong in your own world, and you / might quickly make it right.
Why, the wrong is only a wrong in the world's eyes. And if you get the world for your trouble, it's a wrong in your own world, and you could quickly make it right.
I do not think there is any such woman.
I don't think there's any such woman.

Yes, a dozen, and as many to the vantage as would store the / world they played for. / But I do think it is their husbands' faults / If wives do fall; say that they slack their duties / And pour our treasures into foreign laps, / Or else break out in peevish jealousies, / Throwing restraint upon us, or say they strike us, / Or scant our former having in despite, / Why, we have galls, and though we have some grace, / Yet have we some revenge. Let husbands know / Their wives have sense like them; they see and smell / And have their palates both for sweet and sour, / As husbands have. What is it that they do / When they change us for others? Is it sport? / I think it is. And doth affection breed it? / I think it doth. Is't frailty that thus errs? / It is so too. And have not we affections, / Desires for sport, and frailty, as men have? / Then let them use us well; else let them know, / The ills we do, their ills instruct us so.

Yes, a dozen, and as many more as would fill the world they gambled for. But I do think it's the husbands' fault when wives go wrong. Say they neglect their duties and pour what's ours into other women's laps; or they break out in petty jealousy and lock us up; or say they hit us, or cut our allowance out of spite. Why, we have tempers, and though we have some kindness, we can also take revenge. Husbands should know their wives have senses like them. They see and smell and have tastes for both sweet and sour, just like husbands. What are they doing when they trade us for other women? Is it for fun? I think it is. Does desire drive it? I think it does. Is it weakness that makes them stray? That too. And don't we have desires, a wish for fun, and weakness, just like men? So let them treat us well. Otherwise, let them know that the wrongs we do, they taught us.
Good night, good night. Heaven me such uses send, / Not to pick bad from bad, but by bad mend!
Good night, good night. May heaven help me not to learn bad from bad, but to become better because of it!

Here, stand behind this bulk; straight will he come. / Wear thy good rapier bare, and put it home. / Quick, quick; fear nothing; I'll be at thy elbow. / It makes us, or it mars us; think on that, / And fix most firm thy resolution.

Here, stand behind this wall. He'll be here any minute. Have your sword drawn, and drive it in deep. Quick, quick. Don't be afraid; I'll be right beside you. This makes us or breaks us. Think about that, and keep your resolve firm.
Be near at hand; I may miscarry in't.
Stay close. I might mess it up.
Here, at thy hand, be bold, and take thy stand. / [Retires.]
I'm right here, close at hand. Be brave and take your position. [He steps back.]
I have no great devotion to the deed; / And yet he hath given me satisfying reasons. / 'Tis but a man gone. Forth, my sword; he dies.
I'm not very keen on doing this, and yet he's given me convincing reasons. It's just one man gone. Out, my sword. He dies.

I have rubb'd this young quat almost to the sense, / And he grows angry. Now, whether he kill Cassio, / Or Cassio him, or each do kill the other, / Every way makes my gain. Live Roderigo, / He calls me to a restitution large / Of gold and jewels that I bobb'd from him, / As gifts to Desdemona; / It must not be. If Cassio do remain, / He hath a daily beauty in his life / That makes me ugly; and besides, the Moor / May unfold me to him; there stand I in much peril. / No, he must die. Be't so. I hear him coming.

I've rubbed this young pimple almost raw, and he's getting angry. Now, whether he kills Cassio, or Cassio kills him, or they kill each other, I win either way. If Roderigo lives, he'll demand I pay back all the gold and jewels I swindled from him as gifts for Desdemona. That can't happen. If Cassio survives, he has a daily goodness in his life that makes me look ugly. Besides, the Moor might reveal my story to him, and then I'm in great danger. No, he has to die. So be it. I hear him coming.
I know his gait; 'tis he. Villain, thou diest!
I know his walk. It's him. Villain, you die!
That thrust had been mine enemy indeed, / But that my coat is better than thou know'st; / I will make proof of thine. [Draws, and wounds Roderigo.]
That thrust would have been the end of me if my coat weren't stronger than you think. Now I'll test yours. [He draws and wounds Roderigo.]
I am maim'd forever. Help, ho! Murther! Murther! / [Falls.]
I'm crippled for life. Help! Murder! Murder! [He falls.]
The voice of Cassio; Iago keeps his word.
That's Cassio's voice. Iago is keeping his word.
Oh, what a villain I am!
O, help, ho! Light! A surgeon!
Oh, help! A light! A doctor!

'Tis he. O brave Iago, honest and just, / That hast such noble sense of thy friend's wrong! / Thou teachest me. Minion, your dear lies dead, / And your unblest fate hies. Strumpet, I come! / Forth of my heart those charms, thine eyes, are blotted; / Thy bed lust-stain'd shall with lust's blood be spotted.

It's him. Oh, brave Iago, honest and fair, who feels his friend's wrong so nobly! You're teaching me. You slut, your lover lies dead, and your own cursed fate is coming fast. Whore, I'm coming! Those charms of yours, your eyes, are wiped from my heart. Your bed, stained with lust, will be spattered with lust's blood.
What, ho! No watch? No passage? Murther! Murther!
Hey! No watchmen? No one passing by? Murder! Murder!
'Tis some mischance; the cry is very direful.
Something bad has happened. That cry sounds terrible.
Two or three groan; it is a heavy night. / These may be counterfeits; let's think't unsafe / To come in to the cry without more help.
Two or three people are groaning. It's a dark night. These could be fakes; let's not risk going toward the cries without more help.
Nobody come? Then shall I bleed to death.
Is nobody coming? Then I'll bleed to death.
Here's one comes in his shirt, with light and weapons.
Someone's coming in his shirt, with a light and weapons.
Who's there? Whose noise is this that cries on murther?
Who's there? Who's making this noise, shouting murder?
Did not you hear a cry?
Didn't you hear someone cry out?
Here, here! for heaven's sake, help me!
Here, here! For heaven's sake, help me!
This is Othello's ancient, as I take it.
I think this is Othello's ensign.
The same indeed; a very valiant fellow.
It is. A very brave fellow.
What are you here that cry so grievously?
Who's there, crying out so painfully?
Iago? O, I am spoil'd, undone by villains! / Give me some help.
Iago? Oh, I've been ruined, destroyed by villains! Help me.
O me, lieutenant! What villains have done this?
Oh no, lieutenant! What villains did this?
I think that one of them is hereabout, / And cannot make away.
I think one of them is around here and can't get away.
O treacherous villains! / [To Lodovico and Gratiano.] What are you there? / Come in and give some help.
Oh, treacherous villains! [To Lodovico and Gratiano.] Who are you there? Come here and help.
O damn'd Iago! O inhuman dog!
Oh, damned Iago! Oh, inhuman dog!
Kill men i' the dark! Where be these bloody thieves? / How silent is this town! Ho! Murther! Murther! / What may you be? Are you of good or evil?
Killing men in the dark! Where are these bloody thieves? How quiet this town is! Hey! Murder! Murder! Who are you? Are you good or bad?
As you shall prove us, praise us.
Judge us by what we do.
I cry you mercy. Here's Cassio hurt by villains.
I beg your pardon. Here's Cassio, wounded by villains.
My leg is cut in two.
My leg is cut in two.
Marry, heaven forbid! / Light, gentlemen; I'll bind it with my shirt.
Heaven forbid! A light, gentlemen. I'll bandage it with my shirt.
What is the matter, ho? Who is't that cried?
What's the matter? Who cried out?
O my dear Cassio, my sweet Cassio! O Cassio, Cassio, / Cassio!
Oh, my dear Cassio, my sweet Cassio! Oh, Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!
O notable strumpet! Cassio, may you suspect / Who they should be that have thus mangled you?
Oh, you obvious whore! Cassio, do you have any idea who did this to you?
I am sorry to find you thus; I have been to seek you.
I'm sorry to find you like this. I've been looking for you.
Lend me a garter. So. O, for a chair, / To bear him easily hence!
Give me a garter. There. Oh, if only we had a chair to carry him away gently!
Alas, he faints! O Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!
Oh no, he's fainting! Oh, Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!

Gentlemen all, I do suspect this trash / To be a party in this injury. / Patience awhile, good Cassio. Come, come; / Lend me a light. Know we this face or no? / Alas, my friend and my dear countryman / Roderigo? No- yes, sure. O heaven! Roderigo.

Gentlemen, I suspect this trash had a part in this attack. Be patient a little while, good Cassio. Come, come, give me a light. Do we know this face or not? Oh no, my friend and dear countryman Roderigo? No... yes, it is. Oh heaven! Roderigo.
Even he, sir. Did you know him?
The very same, sir. Did you know him?
Signior Gratiano? I cry you gentle pardon; / These bloody accidents must excuse my manners, / That so neglected you.
Signior Gratiano? I beg your pardon. These bloody events must excuse my bad manners in ignoring you.
I am glad to see you.
How do you, Cassio? O, a chair, a chair!
How are you, Cassio? Oh, a chair, a chair!

He, he, 'tis he. [A chair brought in.] O, that's well said: / the chair. / Some good man bear him carefully from hence; / I'll fetch the general's surgeon. [To Bianca.] For you, mistress, / Save you your labor. He that lies slain here, Cassio, / Was my dear friend; what malice was between you?

It's him, it's him. [A chair is brought in.] Oh, good, the chair. Someone carry him carefully away from here. I'll get the general's surgeon. [To Bianca.] As for you, madam, don't bother. Cassio, the man lying dead here was my dear friend. What quarrel was there between you?
None in the world; nor do I know the man.
None at all. I don't even know the man.
[To Bianca.] What, look you pale? O, bear him out o' the air.
[To Bianca.] What, are you pale? Oh, get him out of the night air.

Stay you, good gentlemen. Look you pale, mistress? / Do you perceive the gastness of her eye? / Nay, if you stare, we shall hear more anon. / Behold her well; I pray you, look upon her. / Do you see, gentlemen? Nay, guiltiness will speak, / Though tongues were out of use.

Stay, good gentlemen. Are you pale, madam? Do you see the terror in her eyes? No, if you stare like that, we'll hear more soon. Look at her closely; please, look at her. Do you see, gentlemen? Guilt will speak for itself, even if no one says a word.
'Las, what's the matter? What's the matter, husband?
Oh no, what's the matter? What's the matter, husband?
Cassio hath here been set on in the dark / By Roderigo, and fellows that are 'scaped; / He's almost slain, and Roderigo dead.
Cassio was attacked here in the dark by Roderigo and some men who escaped. He's nearly dead, and Roderigo is dead.
Alas, good gentleman! alas, good Cassio!
Oh no, the good gentleman! Oh, good Cassio!
This is the fruit of whoring. Prithee, Emilia, / Go know of Cassio where he supp'd tonight. / What, do you shake at that?
This is what comes of whoring. Please, Emilia, go find out from Cassio where he had supper tonight. What, does that make you shake?
He supp'd at my house; but I therefore shake not.
He had supper at my house, but that's not why I'm shaking.
O, did he so? I charge you, go with me.
Oh, did he? I order you to come with me.
I am no strumpet, but of life as honest / As you that thus abuse me.
I'm no whore. I live as honestly as you, who insult me like this.
As I! foh! fie upon thee!
As me! Ugh! Shame on you!

Kind gentlemen, let's go see poor Cassio dress'd. / Come, mistress, you must tell's another tale. / Emilia, run you to the citadel, / And tell my lord and lady what hath happ'd! / Will you go on? [Aside.] This is the night / That either makes me or fordoes me quite.

Kind gentlemen, let's go see poor Cassio's wounds dressed. Come, madam, you'll have to tell us a different story. Emilia, run to the fort and tell my lord and lady what's happened! Will you go ahead? [Aside.] This is the night that either makes me or completely ruins me.

It is the cause, it is the cause, my soul. / Let me not name it to you, you chaste stars! / It is the cause. Yet I'll not shed her blood, / Nor scar that whiter skin of hers than snow / And smooth as monumental alabaster. / Yet she must die, else she'll betray more men. / Put out the light, and then put out the light. / If I quench thee, thou flaming minister, / I can again thy former light restore, / Should I repent me; but once put out thy light, / Thou cunning'st pattern of excelling nature, / I know not where is that Promethean heat / That can thy light relume. When I have pluck'd the rose, / I cannot give it vital growth again, / It must needs wither; I'll smell it on the tree. [Kisses her.] / O, balmy breath, that dost almost persuade / Justice to break her sword! One more, one more; / Be thus when thou art dead, and I will kill thee, / And love thee after. One more, and this the last; / So sweet was ne'er so fatal. I must weep, / But they are cruel tears; this sorrow's heavenly, / It strikes where it doth love. She wakes.

It's the cause, it's the cause, my soul. Let me not name it to you, you chaste stars! It's the cause. Yet I won't shed her blood, or scar that skin of hers, whiter than snow and smooth as marble on a tomb. Yet she must die, or she'll betray more men. Put out the light, and then put out the light. If I put you out, you flaming candle, I can light you again if I change my mind. But once I put out your light, you most perfect model of nature's best work, I don't know where to find the divine fire that could relight you. Once I've picked the rose, I can't make it grow again. It has to wither. I'll smell it while it's still on the bush. [He kisses her.] Oh, sweet breath, that almost persuades Justice to break her sword! One more, one more. Be like this when you're dead, and I'll kill you and love you afterward. One more, and this is the last. Nothing so sweet was ever so deadly. I have to cry, but these are cruel tears. This sorrow is like heaven's: it punishes what it loves. She's waking up.
Will you come to bed, my lord?
Are you coming to bed, my lord?
Have you said your prayers tonight, Desdemona?
If you bethink yourself of any crime / Unreconciled as yet to heaven and grace, / Solicit for it straight.
If you can think of any sin you haven't yet confessed to heaven and been forgiven for, pray for forgiveness right now.
Alas, my lord, what may you mean by that?
Oh, my lord, what do you mean by that?
Well, do it, and be brief; I will walk by. / I would not kill thy unprepared spirit. / No, heaven forfend! I would not kill thy soul.
Well, do it, and be quick. I'll walk over here. I wouldn't want to kill your soul unprepared. No, heaven forbid! I wouldn't kill your soul.
Then heaven have mercy on me!
Then heaven have mercy on me!
If you say so, I hope you will not kill me.
If you say that, I hope you won't kill me.
And yet I fear you, for you are fatal then / When your eyes roll so. Why I should fear I know not, / Since guiltiness I know not; but yet I feel I fear.
And yet I'm afraid of you, because you're deadly when your eyes roll like that. I don't know why I should be afraid, since I know I'm not guilty. But still, I feel afraid.
They are loves I bear to you.
My only sins are the love I have for you.
Ay, and for that thou diest.
Yes, and that's why you die.

That death's unnatural that kills for loving. / Alas, why gnaw you so your nether lip? / Some bloody passion shakes your very frame. / These are portents; but yet I hope, I hope, / They do not point on me.

It's an unnatural death that kills someone for loving. Oh, why are you biting your lower lip like that? Some violent passion is shaking your whole body. These are bad signs. But still I hope, I hope, they aren't aimed at me.
I will so. What's the matter?
That handkerchief which I so loved and gave thee / Thou gavest to Cassio.
That handkerchief that I loved so much and gave you, you gave to Cassio.
No, by my life and soul! / Send for the man, and ask him.
No, I swear on my life and soul! Send for him and ask him.
Sweet soul, take heed, / Take heed of perjury; thou are on thy deathbed.
Sweet soul, be careful. Be careful not to lie under oath. You're on your deathbed.
Ay, but not yet to die.
Yes, but not to die yet.
Yes, presently: / Therefore confess thee freely of thy sin, / For to deny each article with oath / Cannot remove nor choke the strong conception / That I do groan withal. Thou art to die.
Yes, right now. So confess your sin freely, because denying each charge under oath can't remove or smother the strong belief that's tormenting me. You are going to die.
Then Lord have mercy on me!
Then Lord have mercy on me!
And have you mercy too! I never did / Offend you in my life; never loved Cassio / But with such general warranty of heaven / As I might love. I never gave him token.
