And you have mercy too! I never wronged you in my life. I never loved Cassio except in the general way heaven allows. I never gave him any keepsake.
By heaven, I saw my handkerchief in 's hand. / O perjured woman! Thou dost stone my heart, / And makest me call what I intend to do / A murther, which I thought a sacrifice. / I saw the handkerchief.
By heaven, I saw my handkerchief in his hand. Oh, lying woman! You turn my heart to stone, and make me call what I'm going to do a murder, when I thought it was a sacrifice. I saw the handkerchief.
He found it then; / I never gave it him. Send for him hither; / Let him confess a truth.
Then he found it. I never gave it to him. Send for him. Let him confess the truth.
That he has slept with you.
No, his mouth is stopp'd; / Honest Iago hath ta'en order for't.
No, his mouth has been shut. Honest Iago has taken care of that.
O, my fear interprets! What, is he dead?
Oh, my fear tells me what that means! What, is he dead?
Had all his hairs been lives, my great revenge / Had stomach for them all.
If every hair on his head had been a life, my great revenge would have had an appetite for all of them.
Alas, he is betray'd, and I undone!
Oh no, he's been betrayed, and I'm ruined!
Out, strumpet! Weep'st thou for him to my face?
Get out, whore! Are you crying for him to my face?
O, banish me, my lord, but kill me not!
Oh, banish me, my lord, but don't kill me!
Kill me tomorrow; let me live tonight!
Kill me tomorrow; let me live tonight!
Being done, there is no pause.
Now that it's started, there's no stopping.
But while I say one prayer!
Just while I say one prayer!
It is too late. [He stifles her.]
[Within.] My lord, my lord! What, ho! my lord, my lord!
[Offstage.] My lord, my lord! Hello! My lord, my lord!
What noise is this? Not dead? not yet quite dead? / I that am cruel am yet merciful; / I would not have thee linger in thy pain. / So, so.
What's that noise? Not dead? Not quite dead yet? I may be cruel, but I'm still merciful. I don't want you to linger in pain. There, there.
[Within.] What, ho! my lord, my lord!
[Within.] O, good my lord, I would speak a word with you!
[Offstage.] Oh, my good lord, I need to speak with you!

Yes, 'tis Emilia. By and by. She's dead. / 'Tis like she comes to speak of Cassio's death. / The noise was here. Ha! no more moving? / Still as the grave. Shall she come in? were't good? / I think she stirs again. No. What's best to do? / If she come in, she'll sure speak to my wife. / My wife! My wife! What wife? I have no wife. / O, insupportable! O heavy hour! / Methinks it should be now a huge eclipse / Of sun and moon, and that the affrighted globe / Should yawn at alteration.

Yes, it's Emilia. In a moment. She's dead. She's probably coming to tell me about Cassio's death. The noise was loud. Ha! No more moving? Still as the grave. Should I let her in? Would that be wise? I think she's moving again. No. What's the best thing to do? If she comes in, she'll certainly speak to my wife. My wife! My wife! What wife? I have no wife. Oh, unbearable! Oh, terrible hour! I think there should be a huge eclipse of the sun and moon right now, and the terrified earth should split open at this change.
[Within.] I do beseech you / That I may speak with you, O, good my lord!
[Offstage.] I beg you, let me speak with you. Oh, my good lord!
I had forgot thee. O, come in, Emilia. / Soft, by and by. Let me the curtains draw. / Where art thou? [Unlocks the door.]
I forgot about you. Oh, come in, Emilia. Wait, just a moment. Let me close the bed curtains. Where are you? [He unlocks the door.]
What's the matter with thee now?
What's the matter with you now?
O, my good lord, yonder's foul murthers done!
Oh, my good lord, terrible murders have been committed out there!
It is the very error of the moon; / She comes more nearer earth than she was wont / And makes men mad.
It's the moon going off course. She's come closer to the earth than usual, and it drives men mad.
Cassio, my lord, hath kill'd a young Venetian / Call'd Roderigo.
My lord, Cassio has killed a young Venetian named Roderigo.
Not Cassio kill'd! Then murther's out of tune, / And sweet revenge grows harsh.
Cassio's not killed! Then murder is out of tune, and sweet revenge turns harsh.
Oh no, what was that cry?
Out, and alas! That was my lady's voice. / Help! help, ho! help! O lady, speak again! / Sweet Desdemona! O sweet mistress, speak!
Oh, no! That was my lady's voice. Help! Help! Help! Oh, lady, speak again! Sweet Desdemona! Oh, sweet mistress, speak!
O, who hath done this deed?
Nobody; I myself. Farewell; / Commend me to my kind lord. O, farewell! [Dies.]
No one. I did it myself. Goodbye. Give my love to my kind husband. Oh, goodbye! [She dies.]
Why, how should she be murther'd?
Why, how could she have been murdered?
You heard her say herself, it was not I.
You heard her say it herself: it wasn't me.
She said so; I must needs report the truth.
She said so. I have to report the truth.
She's like a liar gone to burning hell; / 'Twas I that kill'd her.
She's gone to burning hell like the liar she was. It was I who killed her.
O, the more angel she, / And you the blacker devil!
Oh, then she's even more of an angel, and you're an even blacker devil!
She turn'd to folly, and she was a whore.
She turned to sin, and she was a whore.
Thou dost belie her, and thou art a devil.
You're lying about her, and you're a devil.
She was as unfaithful as water.
Thou art rash as fire, to say / That she was false. O, she was heavenly true!
You're as reckless as fire to say she was unfaithful. Oh, she was heavenly true!
Cassio did top her; ask thy husband else. / O, I were damn'd beneath all depth in hell, / But that I did proceed upon just grounds / To this extremity. Thy husband knew it all.
Cassio slept with her. Ask your husband if you don't believe me. Oh, I'd be damned to the lowest depths of hell if I hadn't had good reason to go this far. Your husband knew all about it.
That she was false to wedlock?
That she was unfaithful to her marriage?
Ay, with Cassio. Nay, had she been true, / If heaven would make me such another world / Of one entire and perfect chrysolite, / I'ld not have sold her for it.
Yes, with Cassio. No, if she'd been faithful, I wouldn't have traded her even if heaven had made me another world out of a single perfect jewel.
Ay, 'twas he that told me first. / An honest man he is, and hates the slime / That sticks on filthy deeds.
Yes, he was the one who told me first. He's an honest man, and he hates the filth that sticks to dirty deeds.
What needs this iteration, woman? I say thy husband.
Why do you keep repeating it, woman? I said your husband.
O mistress, villainy hath made mocks with love! / My husband say that she was false!
Oh, mistress, villainy has made a mockery of love! My husband said she was unfaithful!
He, woman; / I say thy husband. Dost understand the word? / My friend, thy husband, honest, honest Iago.
Him, woman. I said your husband. Do you understand the word? My friend, your husband, honest, honest Iago.
If he say so, may his pernicious soul / Rot half a grain a day! He lies to the heart. / She was too fond of her most filthy bargain.
If he says so, may his evil soul rot a little bit every day! He's lying through his teeth. She loved her filthy bargain far too much.
Do thy worst; / This deed of thine is no more worthy heaven / Than thou wast worthy her.
Do your worst. This deed of yours is no more worthy of heaven than you were worthy of her.

Thou hast not half that power to do me harm / As I have to be hurt. O gull! O dolt! / As ignorant as dirt! Thou hast done a deed- / I care not for thy sword; I'll make thee known, / Though I lost twenty lives. Help! help, ho! help! / The Moor hath kill'd my mistress! Murther, murther!

You don't have half the power to hurt me that I have to endure it. Oh, you idiot! You fool! As ignorant as dirt! You've done a deed... I don't care about your sword. I'll expose you, even if I lose twenty lives. Help! Help! Help! The Moor has killed my mistress! Murder, murder!
What is the matter? How now, general?
What's the matter? What's going on, general?
O, are you come, Iago? You have done well, / That men must lay their murthers on your neck.
Oh, there you are, Iago? You've done well, so that men have to blame you for their murders.
Disprove this villain, if thou be'st a man. / He says thou told'st him that his wife was false; / I know thou didst not, thou'rt not such a villain. / Speak, for my heart is full.
Prove this villain wrong, if you're a man. He says you told him his wife was unfaithful. I know you didn't; you're not that kind of villain. Speak, because my heart is about to burst.
I told him what I thought, and told no more / Than what he found himself was apt and true.
I told him what I thought, and told him nothing more than what he found to be plausible and true himself.
But did you ever tell him she was false?
But did you ever tell him she was unfaithful?
You told a lie, an odious, damned lie; / Upon my soul, a lie, a wicked lie! / She false with Cassio? Did you say with Cassio?
You told a lie, a hateful, damned lie. I swear on my soul, a lie, a wicked lie! She was unfaithful with Cassio? Did you say with Cassio?
With Cassio, mistress. Go to, charm your tongue.
With Cassio, woman. Go on, hold your tongue.
I will not charm my tongue; I am bound to speak. / My mistress here lies murther'd in her bed-
I won't hold my tongue. I have to speak. My mistress is lying here murdered in her bed—
And your reports have set the murther on.
And your stories led to the murder.
Nay, stare not, masters; it is true indeed.
No, don't stare, gentlemen. It's true.
Villainy, villainy, villainy! / I think upon't, I think, I smell't, O villainy! / I thought so then. I'll kill myself for grief. / O villainy, villainy!
Villainy, villainy, villainy! I'm thinking about it, I'm thinking, I can smell it. Oh, villainy! I suspected it back then. I'll kill myself with grief. Oh, villainy, villainy!
What, are you mad? I charge you, get you home.
What, are you crazy? I order you, go home.
Good gentlemen, let me have leave to speak; / 'Tis proper I obey him, but not now. / Perchance, Iago, I will ne'er go home.
Good gentlemen, let me speak. It's right for me to obey him, but not now. Maybe, Iago, I'll never go home.
O! O! O! [Falls on the bed.]
Oh! Oh! Oh! [He falls on the bed.]
Nay, lay thee down and roar; / For thou hast kill'd the sweetest innocent / That e'er did lift up eye.
Yes, lie down and roar, because you've killed the sweetest innocent woman who ever looked up to heaven.
[Rises.] O, she was foul! / I scarce did know you, uncle; there lies your niece, / Whose breath indeed these hands have newly stopp'd. / I know this act shows horrible and grim.
[Standing.] Oh, she was filthy! I hardly recognized you, uncle. There lies your niece, whose breath these hands have just stopped. I know this looks horrible and grim.

Poor Desdemon! I am glad thy father's dead. / Thy match was mortal to him, and pure grief / Shore his old thread in twain; did he live now, / This sight would make him do a desperate turn, / Yea, curse his better angel from his side, / And fall to reprobation.

Poor Desdemona! I'm glad your father's dead. Your marriage killed him; pure grief cut his old thread of life in two. If he were alive now, this sight would drive him to some desperate act. He'd curse his guardian angel away and fall into damnation.

'Tis pitiful, but yet Iago knows / That she with Cassio hath the act of shame / A thousand times committed. Cassio confess'd it, / And she did gratify his amorous works / With that recognizance and pledge of love / Which I first gave her. I saw it in his hand, / It was a handkerchief, an antique token / My father gave my mother.

It's pitiful. But Iago knows that she committed the shameful act with Cassio a thousand times. Cassio confessed it. And she rewarded his lovemaking with the keepsake and token of love I first gave her. I saw it in his hand. It was a handkerchief, an old token my father gave my mother.
'Twill out, 'twill. I peace? / No, I will speak as liberal as the north; / Let heaven and men and devils, let them all, / All, all, cry shame against me, yet I'll speak.
It'll come out, it will. Me, be quiet? No, I'll speak as freely as the north wind. Let heaven and men and devils, let all of them, all, all, cry shame on me, and I'll still speak.
Be wise, and get you home.
Fie! / Your sword upon a woman?
Shame! Drawing your sword on a woman?

O thou dull Moor! That handkerchief thou speak'st of / I found by fortune and did give my husband, / For often with a solemn earnestness, / More than indeed belong'd to such a trifle, / He begg'd of me to steal it.

Oh, you stupid Moor! That handkerchief you're talking about, I found by chance and gave to my husband. Because he often begged me, with a seriousness far too great for such a trivial thing, to steal it.
She give it Cassio? No, alas, I found it, / And I did give't my husband.
She gave it to Cassio? No, I found it, and I gave it to my husband.
By heaven, I do not, I do not, gentlemen. / O murtherous coxcomb! What should such a fool / Do with so good a wife?
By heaven, I'm not, I'm not, gentlemen. Oh, murderous idiot! What was a fool like you doing with such a good wife?
Are there not stones in heaven / But what serve for thunder? Precious villain!
Aren't there any thunderbolts in heaven except the ones used for thunder? Absolute villain!
The woman falls; sure, he hath kill'd his wife.
The woman's falling. He must have killed his wife.
Ay, ay! O, lay me by my mistress' side.
Yes, yes! Oh, lay me beside my mistress.
He's gone, but his wife's kill'd.
He's gone, but his wife is killed.

'Tis a notorious villain. Take you this weapon, / Which I have here recover'd from the Moor. / Come, guard the door without; let him not pass, / But kill him rather. I'll after that same villain, / For 'tis a damned slave.

He's an infamous villain. Take this weapon, which I've just taken from the Moor. Come, guard the door from outside. Don't let him pass; kill him first. I'll go after that villain, because he's a damned slave.
I am not valiant neither, / But every puny whipster gets my sword. / But why should honor outlive honesty? / Let it go all.
I'm not brave anymore either; any puny little fighter can take my sword. But why should my reputation outlive my honor? Let it all go.

What did thy song bode, lady? / Hark, canst thou hear me? I will play the swan, / And die in music. [Sings.] "Willow, willow, willow." / Moor, she was chaste; she loved thee, cruel Moor; / So come my soul to bliss, as I speak true; / So speaking as I think, I die, I die. [Dies.]

What did your song predict, lady? Listen, can you hear me? I'll be like the swan and die singing. [Singing.] "Willow, willow, willow." Moor, she was chaste. She loved you, cruel Moor. May my soul go to heaven as I'm telling the truth. Saying what I believe, I die, I die. [She dies.]
I have another weapon in this chamber; / It is a sword of Spain, the ice-brook's temper- / O, here it is. Uncle, I must come forth.
I have another weapon in this room. It's a Spanish sword, tempered in icy water. Oh, here it is. Uncle, I have to come out.
[Within.] If thou attempt it, it will cost thee dear. / Thou hast no weapon, and perforce must suffer.
[Offstage.] If you try, it'll cost you. You have no weapon, so you'll have to accept what happens.
Look in upon me then, and speak with me, / Or, naked as I am, I will assault thee.
Then come in and talk to me, or, unarmed as I am, I'll attack you.

Behold, I have a weapon; / A better never did itself sustain / Upon a soldier's thigh. I have seen the day / That with this little arm and this good sword / I have made my way through more impediments / Than twenty times your stop. But, O vain boast! / Who can control his fate? 'Tis not so now. / Be not afraid, though you do see me weapon'd; / Here is my journey's end, here is my butt / And very sea-mark of my utmost sail. / Do you go back dismay'd? 'Tis a lost fear. / Man but a rush against Othello's breast, / And he retires. Where should Othello go? / Now, how dost thou look now? O ill-starr'd wench! / Pale as thy smock! When we shall meet at compt, / This look of thine will hurl my soul from heaven, / And fiends will snatch at it. Cold, cold, my girl? / Even like thy chastity. O cursed, cursed slave! / Whip me, ye devils, / From the possession of this heavenly sight! / Blow me about in winds! Roast me in sulphur! / Wash me in steep-down gulfs of liquid fire! / O Desdemon! dead, Desdemon! dead! / O! O! O!

Look, I have a weapon. A better one never hung at a soldier's side. I've seen the day when, with this little arm and this good sword, I fought my way through obstacles twenty times stronger than you. But, oh, what an empty boast! Who can control his fate? It's not like that now. Don't be afraid, even though you see me armed. This is the end of my journey, my final goal, the landmark of my last voyage. Are you backing away in fear? There's no need. Just point a reed at Othello's chest, and he'll retreat. Where would Othello go? Now, how do you look now? Oh, unlucky girl! Pale as your nightgown! When we meet on Judgment Day, this look of yours will hurl my soul out of heaven, and devils will snatch it up. Cold, cold, my girl? Just like your chastity. Oh, cursed, cursed slave that I am! Whip me, you devils, away from the sight of this heavenly creature! Blow me around in the winds! Roast me in sulfur! Wash me in deep pits of liquid fire! Oh, Desdemona! Dead, Desdemona! Dead! Oh! Oh! Oh!
Where is this rash and most unfortunate man?
Where is this reckless and most unfortunate man?
That's he that was Othello. Here I am.
That's the man who used to be Othello. Here I am.
Where is that viper? Bring the villain forth.
Where's that snake? Bring the villain forward.
I look down towards his feet; but that's a fable. / If that thou be'st a devil, I cannot kill thee. [Wounds Iago.]
I look down at his feet to see if they're cloven, but that's just a fairy tale. If you're a devil, I can't kill you. [He wounds Iago.]
I bleed, sir, but not kill'd.
I'm bleeding, sir, but not dead.
I am not sorry neither. I'ld have thee live, / For, in my sense, 'tis happiness to die.
I'm not sorry about that. I'd rather you live, because the way I feel, it's happiness to die.
O thou Othello, that wert once so good, / Fall'n in the practice of a damned slave, / What shall be said to thee?
Oh, Othello, you who were once so good, caught in the trap of a damned slave, what can we say to you?
Why, anything; / An honorable murtherer, if you will, / For nought did I in hate, but all in honor.
Why, anything. An honorable murderer, if you like, because I did nothing out of hate, but all for honor.
This wretch hath part confess'd his villainy. / Did you and he consent in Cassio's death?
This wretch has partly confessed his villainy. Did you and he agree to kill Cassio?
Dear general, I never gave you cause.
Dear general, I never gave you any reason.
I do believe it, and I ask your pardon. / Will you, I pray, demand that demi-devil / Why he hath thus ensnared my soul and body?
I believe it, and I ask your forgiveness. Will you please ask that half-devil why he trapped my soul and body like this?
Demand me nothing; what you know, you know. / From this time forth I never will speak word.
Don't ask me anything. What you know, you know. From now on, I'll never say a word.
Well, that's the best thing you can do.

Sir, you shall understand what hath befall'n, / Which, as I think, you know not. Here is a letter / Found in the pocket of the slain Roderigo, / And here another. The one of them imports / The death of Cassio to be undertook / By Roderigo.

Sir, you'll understand what has happened, which I don't think you know yet. Here's a letter found in the pocket of the dead Roderigo, and here's another. One of them says that Roderigo was to kill Cassio.

Now here's another discontented paper, / Found in his pocket too; and this, it seems, / Roderigo meant to have sent this damned villain; / But that, belike, Iago in the interim / Came in and satisfied him.
Now here's another angry letter, also found in his pocket. It seems Roderigo meant to send it to this damned villain, but Iago probably came along in the meantime and calmed him down.
O the pernicious caitiff! / How came you, Cassio, by that handkerchief / That was my wife's?
Oh, the evil wretch! Cassio, how did you get that handkerchief that was my wife's?
I found it in my chamber; / And he himself confess'd but even now / That there he dropp'd it for a special purpose / Which wrought to his desire.
I found it in my room. And he himself confessed just now that he dropped it there for a specific purpose, which worked out the way he wanted.

There is besides in Roderigo's letter, / How he upbraids Iago, that he made him / Brave me upon the watch, whereon it came / That I was cast. And even but now he spake / After long seeming dead, Iago hurt him, / Iago set him on.

Roderigo's letter also says that he blamed Iago for making him provoke me while I was on watch, which led to my being dismissed. And just now, after seeming to be dead for a long time, he said that Iago had stabbed him, and that Iago put him up to it.

You must forsake this room, and go with us. / Your power and your command is taken off, / And Cassio rules in Cyprus. For this slave, / If there be any cunning cruelty / That can torment him much and hold him long, / It shall be his. You shall close prisoner rest, / Till that the nature of your fault be known / To the Venetian state. Come, bring away.

You have to leave this room and come with us. Your power and command are taken away, and Cassio rules in Cyprus. As for this slave, if there's any clever cruelty that can torture him a lot and keep him alive a long time, it will be his. You will remain a closely guarded prisoner until the Venetian government learns the nature of your crime. Come, bring him away.

Soft you; a word or two before you go. / I have done the state some service, and they know't. / No more of that. I pray you, in your letters, / When you shall these unlucky deeds relate, / Speak of me as I am; nothing extenuate, / Nor set down aught in malice. Then must you speak / Of one that loved not wisely but too well; / Of one not easily jealous, but, being wrought, / Perplex'd in the extreme; of one whose hand, / Like the base Indian, threw a pearl away / Richer than all his tribe; of one whose subdued eyes, / Albeit unused to the melting mood, / Drop tears as fast as the Arabian trees / Their medicinal gum. Set you down this; / And say besides, that in Aleppo once, / Where a malignant and a turban'd Turk / Beat a Venetian and traduced the state, / I took by the throat the circumcised dog / And smote him, thus. [Stabs himself.]

Wait. A word or two before you go. I've done the state some service, and they know it. Enough of that. I ask you, in your letters, when you report these unhappy events, describe me as I am. Don't make excuses for me, and don't write anything out of malice. Then you must speak of a man who loved not wisely but too well; of a man not easily made jealous, but who, once manipulated, was driven to extreme confusion; of a man whose hand, like the ignorant Indian, threw away a pearl worth more than his whole tribe; of a man whose defeated eyes, though not used to weeping, now drop tears as fast as Arabian trees drip their healing gum. Write that down. And say also that once in Aleppo, when a hostile, turbaned Turk beat a Venetian and insulted the state, I took the circumcised dog by the throat and struck him, like this. [He stabs himself.]
I kiss'd thee ere I kill'd thee. No way but this, / Killing myself, to die upon a kiss.
I kissed you before I killed you. There's no other way than this: killing myself, to die upon a kiss.
This did I fear, but thought he had no weapon; / For he was great of heart.
I was afraid of this, but I thought he had no weapon. He had a great heart.

[To Iago.] O Spartan dog, / More fell than anguish, hunger, or the sea! / Look on the tragic loading of this bed; / This is thy work. The object poisons sight; / Let it be hid. Gratiano, keep the house, / And seize upon the fortunes of the Moor, / For they succeed on you. To you, Lord Governor, / Remains the censure of this hellish villain, / The time, the place, the torture. O, enforce it! / Myself will straight aboard, and to the state / This heavy act with heavy heart relate.

[To Iago.] Oh, you vicious dog, more cruel than pain, hunger, or the sea! Look at the tragic load on this bed. This is your work. The sight poisons the eyes; cover it up. Gratiano, take charge of the house and take possession of the Moor's property, because you inherit it. To you, Lord Governor, falls the sentencing of this hellish villain: the time, the place, the torture. Oh, carry it out! I'll go aboard ship right away, and with a heavy heart report this heavy deed to the state.
